candidates.title: Large Language Models in Fruit Science
candidates.abstract: This chapter reviews large language models (LLMs) applications and future prospects in fruit sciences. LLMs are advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models trained on extensive datasets, and are revolutionizing how fruit scientists and agriculturists interact with and analyze data. Analysis of genetic data, interpretation of climate data, and forecasting of market trends are some of the topics that are covered. These models make it easier to automate the annotation of data, improve decision support systems for precision agriculture, and reveal client preferences and market behaviors for forecasting. In addition, the ethical implications and difficulties that are linked with the deployment of LLMs are elaborated. Case studies from the real world, such as AI-powered pest monitoring and irrigation systems, are presented to illustrate the practical advantages of LLMs in terms of increasing yield, lowering resource use, and improving the overall efficiency of fruit production. LLMs will be integrated into fruit science in the future, but more research and collaboration are needed to maximize their potential in this dynamic sector.

candidates.title: Large Language Models for Forecasting of Electricity Price Spikes
candidates.abstract: Can market notices read by a large language model (LLM) improve short-horizon electricity price spike forecasts? We study five regions of Australia's National Electricity Market. A local LLM extracted features once per notice, only notices visible at the forecast origin were used, and a gradient-boosting model produced onset probabilities. In an out-of-sample development back-test (July 2022 to July 2024), notice features did not lower the 60-minute Brier score of a numeric model including the market operator's next-hour forecasts. At 24 hours they did, but rule-based features did so almost equally and attribution to notice content was not established. A locally frozen protocol, not publicly deposited, governed a retrospective single-use holdout from 15 August to 17 October 2026. At 60 minutes, the hypothesis that LLM features lower the numeric model's Brier score was not established (H1; relative Brier skill -0.09%), so the planned comparison with rule-based features was not tested (H2). At 24 hours, the hypothesis that LLM features lower the score against a text-free control was not established (H3; +0.37%, 95% CI [-9.74, 1.39], inconclusive). By the frozen wording rule the non-significant 24-hour improvement comes mainly from recalibration and cannot be attributed to notice content, although post hoc the decomposition could not separate recalibration from resolution. The 24-hour base rate was 1.56% on the holdout against 14.0% in development. With 5 onsets on 3 days and 24-hour positives in 2 of 22 three-day blocks, the holdout neither established nor excluded a 24-hour effect.

candidates.title: Large Language Model-Assisted Adaptive Heuristic Search for Agile Earth Observation Satellite Scheduling
candidates.abstract: Agile Earth observation satellites must coordinate imaging tasks within limited observation windows, while accounting for attitude maneuvering and onboard energy constraints. Competition among observation opportunities makes scheduling performance sensitive to the heuristic rules used for task selection. This letter proposes a large language model (LLM)-assisted adaptive heuristic search method for agile Earth observation satellite scheduling. The LLM generates an initial heuristic rule according to the characteristics of the scheduling instance. During the subsequent ant colony search, search performance and scheduling information are fed back to the LLM to refine the heuristic rule. The proposed modifications are evaluated through paired solution constructions before being incorporated into the search process. A unified scheduling procedure determines task selection, satellite assignment, and observation timing under the operational constraints. Experiments on six scheduling scenarios involving 50--200 imaging tasks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 4.3\%--9.6\% higher mean observation benefit than the strongest baseline.

candidates.title: Large Language Model Use in Agronomy
candidates.abstract: This study explores how large language models (LLMs) can transform agronomic research and precision agriculture. As the fourth paradigm in agriculture, following mechanization, chemical usage, and genetic interventions, LLMs are poised to revolutionize farming practices. In soil and crop management, LLMs offer context-specific advice for tasks such as weed control, nutrient management, irrigation scheduling, plant scouting, and disease diagnosis, leading to improved resource efficiency, higher crop yields, and enhanced environmental sustainability. The study also highlights LLMs’ promise in tracking crop health and estimating yield. By leveraging hyperspectral imaging and deep learning techniques, LLMs can accurately assess crop stress, disease, and growth stages. For yield prediction, combining LLMs with biophysical crop models and multidimensional data offers a sophisticated approach to understand complex crop–environment interactions. Furthermore, LLMs are being adopted in various agricultural domains, including smart livestock farming, precision aquaculture, and agricultural extension services. They offer personalized advice to farmers, interpret satellite imagery, and even assist in coding and experimental design. However, challenges persist in data quality, privacy, scalability, and ethical concerns. The research underscores the need for collaborative efforts between agronomists, digital designers, and other stakeholders to 178 fully realize LLMs’ potential. It suggests that by integrating LLMs with traditional wisdom and improving data management, agronomists can pioneer a new paradigm in their field. As LLMs mature, they exhibit the promise of significantly enhancing agronomic skills, driving sustainable farming practices, and ultimately contributing to global food security.

candidates.title: Insect Study Through Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), a type of artificial intelligence, mimic human language patterns, enabling comprehension, prediction, and generation of valuable content. In agricultural entomology—the study of insects—LLMs like ChatGPT offer transformative potential for education and research. They simplify complex topics such as insect ecology, life stages, integrated pest management, and species identification, making them accessible for teaching and learning. LLMs assist educators by reducing workload in curriculum design, grading, and developing engaging teaching strategies for practical activities. These technologies enhance knowledge sharing, scientific writing, and research in insect–plant interactions. This chapter explores the role of LLMs in advancing pedagogy, improving insect and pest identification, and addressing ethical concerns and challenges with their application in entomology. By leveraging LLMs, educators and researchers can revolutionize approaches to agricultural entomology, enriching both teaching and scientific exploration.

candidates.title: FourSight: Stable FP4 RL Post-Training via Sequence Filtering and Sparse Channel Compensation
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training increasingly targets low-bit deployment, with NVFP4 weight-and activation quantization (W4A4) becoming the state-of-the-practice format. However, integrating NVFP4 into RL degrades rollout quality and amplifies cross-engine training-inference mismatch (TIM), destabilizing training. We show that these failures are concentrated rather than uniform - severely mismatched tail tokens concentrate in a few outlier sequences, while policy weights remain largely intact and quantization error concentrates in a few high-variance activation channels. Guided by this, we present FourSight, an algorithm-system co-design with two targeted solutions: TIM-aware sequence filtering that excludes drifted trajectories from policy updates, and sparse precision compensation that keeps only top-variance channels in BF16 while retaining native NVFP4 elsewhere. We further design a fused SpliceGEMM kernel with specialized prefill and decode datapaths to minimize overhead. FourSight sustains near-BF16 accuracy and strong FP4 deployment quality across models and engines, while improving step-to-accuracy by 1.76-2.60x and staying within 2.3% of FP4 step time up to 120B-scale models.

candidates.title: Filter-then-match: Holistic Schema Matching via Small Language Model Filtering and Large Language Model Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Schema matching (SM) is a critical step in data integration pipelines and serves as a foundation for tasks such as Table Search and Entity Matching. However, applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to SM is prohibitively expensive due to the task's inherent quadratic complexity, which hinders scalable and cost-efficient deployment. In this paper, we investigate two SM scenarios: the most common instance-based scenario where headers and their values are available, and the metadata-based scenario where only metadata is provided (e.g., due to privacy constraints). We propose Fermat, a unified framework designed to address both scenarios effectively. Fermat incorporates a Small Language Model (SLM)-based filtering strategy that significantly reduce the computational overhead of applying LLMs to SM. We also introduce a column synthesis workflow that enables a fully unsupervised solution, effectively mitigating the scarcity of ground-truth data. Additionally, we implement a specialized loss function with hard column mining to counteract the biases of the filter model on imbalanced data, ensuring improved recall of positive candidates. Finally, we conduct comprehensive reproduction and evaluation of recent schema matching methods on both metadata-based and instance-based datasets, providing insights into their generalizability across diverse scenarios.

candidates.title: Evolution of Large Language Models and Agricultural Sciences
candidates.abstract: Imagine a world where humans and computers converse as rapidly as friends. OpenAI’s Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT) models are creating this future by giving gadgets human-like conversational skills. GPT-4 and other GPT models represent some of the newest advances in artificial intelligence (AI). These are large language models (LLMs) that are trained using extensive datasets to understand and generate text that creates human-like text with great precision. These AI models will have effects that go beyond voice assistants. With OpenAI’s models, developers can now use natural language processing to make apps that decode human wants in ways that were existing in science fiction. One can use GPT-4 and 4 ChatGPT ideas in everything from research paper writing ideas, tools for learning that are tailored to each student. Yet, what do GPT-4 and ChatGPT mean? This chapter introduces the fundamentals, genesis, and key attributes of LLMs and their emerging applications in agricultural sciences.

candidates.title: Collaborative Search Meets Large Language Models: An Empirical Study
candidates.abstract: Collaborative search enables users to address complex information needs jointly. Advances in large language models (LLMs) enable autonomous agents to support collaborative information seeking within shared communication spaces. However, little is known about how these agents shape search experiences, behaviors, and outcomes compared with conventional search tools. We conduct a user study with 80 students working in 40 pairs. Each pair completes four collaborative search tasks under four scenarios: QAAgent, which answers queries using an LLM's parametric knowledge; CoSearchAgent, which uses multi-user conversational context to reformulate queries, retrieve web information, and generate source-grounded answers, while asking clarifying questions when needed; an in-chat search plugin that returns result lists; and manual Google Search. After each task, participants complete several questionnaires assessing their search experience and independently write a report; after all tasks, they participate in individual interviews. Results show that LLM-based agents reduce perceived workload, support collaboration, and reshape communication and evidence-use practices. They also encourage more independent paraphrasing, albeit at the cost of report richness. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic empirical comparison of LLM-based agents and conventional tools for collaborative search across search experience, user behavior, and collaborative outcomes.

candidates.title: Cite Unseen: Measuring Citation-Channel Vulnerabilities in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Citation-grounded retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems expose source URLs alongside answers, extending user trust to cited links. Prior corpus-poisoning research primarily targets answer corruption, overlooking cases where answers remain largely unchanged while citations route users to unsafe destinations. We identify this citation-channel vulnerability and introduce Citation-stage Attack Success Rate (C-ASR) to separate citation manipulation from answer degradation. Across four BEIR corpora, three retrievers, and four generators, changing only the source URL of a single injected document reaches 71% C-ASR on the most vulnerable generator at well under 1% corpus pollution. The attack persists with paraphrased or answer-derived content, while citation behavior differs sharply across generators under our fixed pipeline. These results expose a model-dependent safety surface missed by answer-centric RAG evaluation.

candidates.title: Can Large Language Models Review the Scientific Literature? A Test Against a 102-Article Benchmark
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support scientific literature reviews, yet evaluations often examine individual tasks rather than the review process as a whole. We assess six AI tools across four stages: finding relevant articles, interpreting them, synthesizing across them, and proposing future research. The benchmark is a published review of the Spanish plume weather pattern and its 102-article corpus. In the initial searches, five tools collectively identified 57 articles, with the best individual tool finding 42. Institutional library access increased discovery from 42 to 82 articles for Codex and from 15 to 79 for Claude Code. Given the complete corpus of 102 PDFs, three tools correctly identified all 18 articles discussing the Spanish plume substantially, but incorrectly classified 40% to 79% of the 84 passing mentions as substantial. The same three tools produced syntheses evaluated blindly by two domain experts. Although largely accurate, the syntheses provided limited insight and sometimes contained unsupported claims, quotation errors, and exaggerated statements of consensus. Finally, all three tools proposed research directions broader than the Spanish plume literature, although two approached questions identified in the benchmark review. No single tool performed best across all tasks. We provide eight recommendations for researchers using AI tools in literature reviews. Our findings suggest that LLMs can assist with discovering and interpreting scientific literature, particularly when institutional access is available, but cannot replace expert judgment in evaluating evidence or synthesizing research.

candidates.title: Bilingual and multimodal evaluation of large language models and oral and maxillofacial surgeons for differentiating oral leukoplakia from oral squamous cell carcinoma: a retrospective single-centre disease-enriched diagnostic reader study
candidates.abstract: Differentiating oral leukoplakia from oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is clinically important; however, visual assessment alone can be challenging. This study compared two multimodal large language model (LLM) configurations with two oral and maxillofacial surgeons in a forced binary classification task and examined the effects of histopathological input, prompt language, session protocol, repeatability, and the behaviour of model-reported probability estimates. This retrospective, single-centre, disease-enriched diagnostic reader study was reported in accordance with the STARD 2015 and STARD-AI reporting guidelines. The dataset was deliberately balanced by selecting 50 cases from each diagnostic category (50 oral leukoplakia and 50 OSCC; 100 patients in total); it therefore does not reflect clinical prevalence. Clinical photographs and histopathological regions of interest were retrospectively selected by investigators who were aware of the final clinicopathological diagnosis. Two oral and maxillofacial surgeons and two multimodal LLM configurations (GPT-5.5 Thinking and Gemini 3 Pro) independently classified each case as oral leukoplakia or OSCC under two input conditions: clinical-only information and clinical information supplemented with histopathological images. The final clinicopathological diagnosis issued by the institutional pathology service was used as the reference standard; the histological images presented to evaluators originated from the same specimens used to establish that reference diagnosis. Diagnostic performance, evaluator agreement, OSCC classification tendency, language and session effects, repeatability across five independent runs, and model-reported OSCC probability estimates were analysed. In the clinical-only condition, diagnostic accuracy ranged from 88.0% to 94.0% across evaluators. GPT-5.5 Thinking and Gemini 3 Pro achieved accuracies of 93.0% and 94.0%, respectively, and no statistically significant differences between evaluators were detected after Holm adjustment; the study was not designed as an equivalence or non-inferiority investigation, and these results therefore do not establish equivalent performance. Following the addition of histopathological images, accuracy increased to 99.0%–100.0% across evaluators, with an overall posterior median improvement of + 6.6% points (95% credible interval, + 4.0 to + 10.2). Korean–English prompt differences were small, ranging from 0 to 2% points. In an exploratory single-run comparison, sequential-session evaluation reduced clinical-only accuracy from 93.0% to 78.0% for GPT-5.5 Thinking and from 94.0% to 82.0% for Gemini 3 Pro; because this comparison was based on one run per model, it cannot be distinguished from ordinary stochastic variation and is reported as hypothesis-generating. Across repeated independent runs, case-level stability ranged from 92.0% to 99.0%. Model-reported OSCC probabilities showed high discrimination in the clinical-only condition, whereas calibration could not be reliably assessed in the clinical-plus-histology condition because of near-perfect or perfect separation. Within this selected, balanced, single-centre dataset, no statistically significant difference in diagnostic accuracy was detected between the two multimodal LLM configurations and the two oral and maxillofacial surgeons. These findings should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence or non-inferiority. The near-perfect accuracy observed after histopathological input was obtained in a reader task using representative fields selected from already diagnosed specimens and does not demonstrate general histopathological competence. Session-protocol sensitivity, diagnosis-aware image selection, the restricted diagnostic spectrum, and the limited human comparator group indicate that these results are preliminary and do not support clinical implementation before prospective, externally validated confirmation.

candidates.title: Application of Large Language Models in Agricultural Entomology
candidates.abstract: Agricultural entomology, a critical field focused on the study of insects that affect crop production, benefits greatly from advances in artificial intelligence (AI), by using large language models (LLMs) such as Chat Generative Pre-trained Transformer 4. These models, trained on large datasets, demonstrate remarkable natural language understanding and solution generation capabilities that can be used to address a variety of agricultural entomology challenges. LLMs make it easier to analyze large amounts of entomological literature, allowing researchers to quickly access and synthesize data on insect behavior, pest management strategies, and the ecological impacts of various species. LLMs can also help develop intelligent advisory systems that provide farmers with real-time, data-driven pest control recommendations, thereby improving sustainable agricultural practices. The use of LLMs in predictive modeling improves forecasting pest outbreaks by analyzing climate and environmental data. This chapter investigates the potential applications of LLMs in agricultural entomology, emphasizing their ability to accelerate research, improve decision-making processes, and promote precision agriculture. The discussion will include case studies of successful implementations, challenges in integrating AI with traditional entomological research, and future directions for using LLMs to advanced field. These advanced 94 technologies offer significant advantages in agricultural entomology; their application also presents several drawbacks, which can be balanced by joint approaches that integrate LLMs with human expertise, improve data quality, ensure transparency, and build the necessary infrastructure to support the use of advanced AI in agricultural entomology.

candidates.title: Aligning Training and Rollout Policies for End-to-End FP4 RL on Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
candidates.abstract: In this work, we study end-to-end FP4 reinforcement learning (RL) post-training for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models. Recent work on FP4 RL has introduced effective recovery recipes that restore accuracy under aggressive low-precision quantization for dense models, but we find that the same approach yields no improvement over the naive FP4 baseline in the MoE setting. We conduct an in-depth study to understand why. Our analysis identifies the root cause in the routing mechanism unique to MoE: because the router makes discrete expert-selection decisions, training-inference policy alignment becomes acutely sensitive to whether the same recovery technique is applied symmetrically on the training and inference sides. When an asymmetric recipe is used-including the dense-model approach, which corrects only the rollout-training-inference alignment deteriorates sharply, as measured by the Pearson correlation coefficient between training and inference probabilities, and router selection matching rates. Building on this finding, we propose MoEResQ, a quantization-recovery recipe for MoE RL post-training that enforces symmetry between the training- and inference-side corrections. MoEResQ restores training-inference alignment and substantially closes the accuracy gap to full precision, establishing symmetric recovery as the key principle in FP4 RL for MoE models.

candidates.title: AdSteer: Native Advertising in Large Language Model Generation
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) services face rapidly rising serving costs. To sustain free or affordable access for a broad user base, alternative monetization mechanisms are needed. Native advertising offers a promising approach, as it creates economic value by aligning user intent with merchant offerings. Yet how to integrate sponsored content naturally into LLM responses remains largely underexplored. Existing approaches primarily rely on prompt-level injection, multi-pass rewriting, or fine-tuning, which can compromise response quality or introduce additional computational costs. We propose AdSteer, a lightweight decoding-time advertising framework that adaptively adjusts token probabilities to integrate contextually appropriate advertisement into responses. AdSteer calibrates the strength and duration of advertising influence, making sponsored content a natural part of the response. Experiments on GEM-Bench across three application scenarios show that AdSteer achieves an average improvement of 14.1% in overall score over the strongest baselines and 22.5% fewer total tokens on average than rewrite-based methods. These results demonstrate that AdSteer provides an effective and practical solution for native advertising in LLMs.

candidates.title: TraceRouter++: Causal Semantic Routing Realignment via Optimal Transport
candidates.abstract: Despite their remarkable capabilities, large foundation models (LFMs) remain susceptible to adversarial manipulation. Current safety intervention methods primarily rely on the \textit{locality hypothesis}, rigidly suppressing isolated neurons or features. However, harmful semantics manifest as distributed, cross-layer circuits, rendering localized ablations both brittle against complex jailbreaks and detrimental to general utility. To bridge this gap, we propose TraceRouter++, a routing-level safety intervention framework that explicitly traces safety-relevant causal routing pathways activated under harmful inputs and realigns their unsafe activation states. Our framework operates in a \textit{Discover-Trace-Realign} paradigm: it first pinpoints a sensitive onset layer via attention divergence and disentangles dense activations into interpretable routing features using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Subsequently, it maps these features to downstream causal circuits via feature influence scores (FIS). Crucially, departing from rigid suppression paradigms, TraceRouter++ introduces a constrained optimal transport (OT)-based soft routing realignment. By formulating safety intervention as a tractable coordinate-wise marginal optimal transport approximation, our method redirects unsafe activation marginals toward safe-reference marginals within causally identified routing subspaces while preserving non-selected coordinates at the intervention point. This mechanism safely redirects malicious semantic flows while leaving orthogonal computational routes intact. Extensive experiments across representative large language models (LLMs), multimodal large language models (MLLMs), and diffusion models (DMs) show that TraceRouter++ outperforms evaluated baselines, improving adversarial robustness while maintaining a favorable safety-utility trade-off. candidates.title: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents
candidates.abstract: Large language models are deployed as long-horizon agents that compose diverse tools across MCP services into executable workflows. Existing MCP environment-scaling methods are data-centric: they first synthesize a database and scenario, then derive tools and tasks from them. As a result, tool interfaces may not match real ones, tool compositions are not grounded in execution, and tasks rarely span more than one environment. We propose ToolSpace, a tool-centric framework that reverses this order. ToolSpace mines data, state, and retry dependencies from adjacent calls in execution traces of real MCP services and open agent corpora, using deterministic rules rather than LLM judgment, and clusters the resulting weighted tool-composition graph into environments. Databases are synthesized only for state-mutating environments, while query and stateless tools replay recorded returns. ToolSpace then performs state-aware random walks with rollback and decompiles each chain into a natural-language task with assertion-based checks, keeping only samples that replay successfully from the initial state. Applied to AutomationBench and tau3-Bench Banking, the pipeline produces harder Pro versions on which 7 frontier models drop by up to 38.2 points. Across seven long-horizon tool-use benchmarks, ToolSpace raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 23.0 to 41.0 average score (43.2 with RL) and GLM-5.2 from 44.6 to 56.6, on par with Claude Opus 5. Ablations show that execution-witnessed edges clearly outperform LLM-judged ones, and performance keeps improving with data and environment scale.

candidates.title: Tasks over Application Manuals: Revealing Gaps in Long-Horizon Procedural Reasoning for Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance on a wide range of natural language tasks, and recent benchmarks suggest that they are increasingly adept at multi-hop reasoning. However, these benchmarks are typically short-horizon, requiring only a small number of retrieval or inference steps, and provide limited evidence of reliability on real-world tasks that involve following manuals spanning hundreds of pages with complex, interdependent guidelines. In this paper, we introduce Tasks over Application Manuals (TAM), a benchmark for evaluating long-horizon procedural reasoning. We construct TAM by curating real-world tasks from two domains—ICD-10-CM clinical coding (mapping medical conditions to diagnostic codes) and U.S. federal sentencing (computing crime sentencing guideline outcomes, specifically offense levels)—with human-validated labels. Each task requires following an authoritative manual with tens of thousands of rules and executing a sequence of interdependent steps across different sections to produce an exact answer. We evaluate general-purpose prompting approaches, including retrieval-augmented generation, ReAct-style prompting, and an agent-harness baseline on GPT-5, and find that the best exact-match performance remains extremely low: 1% on ICD-10-CM coding and 15.5% on sentencing tasks. These results show that current benchmarks may overestimate LLM reasoning ability and miss a key challenge: reliably following long, rule-based procedures.

candidates.title: TSFM Meets LLM: Context as Covariates
candidates.abstract: Textual information is ubiquitous in real-world time series datasets, appearing as news, reports, and annotations that hold key predictive signals not deducible from numerical history alone. Large Language Models (LLMs) interpret text but lack numerical precision, while Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) are quantitatively accurate but cannot reason about the effects of text. Moreover, the lack of large-scale paired multimodal datasets limits progress in bridging this gap. In this work, we address this challenge by providing a scalable approach for generating realistic multimodal datasets by annotating real-world time series with LLMs. Building on this, we propose Context as Covariates (CoCo), a forecasting framework in which an LLM distills its textual reasoning into numerically grounded forecast and confidence covariates that guide a TSFM backbone, thereby exploiting the strengths of both LLMs and TSFMs. We align the two models in stages, first fine-tuning the LLM via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a reward tied to covariate-induced improvement in forecasting performance, and then fine-tuning the TSFM on covariates generated by the aligned LLM. Our experiments show that models trained on our synthetic multimodal corpus generalize to real benchmarks spanning finance, economics, weather, traffic, and security. Notably, CoCo with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as the LLM and Chronos2 as the TSFM achieves up to 12% MAE improvement over state-of-the-art TSFMs and LLM forecasters, such as GPT-4o. Code, checkpoints, and the evaluation datasets are publicly available.

candidates.title: Factorized MLLM Embeddings for Composed Image Retrieval
candidates.abstract: Composed Image Retrieval (CIR) aims to retrieve a target image given a reference image and a modification text. Although recent approaches leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown significant progress, we argue that the MLLM's compositional understanding remains underutilized. This stems from directly mapping composed queries into a retrieval embedding via contrastive supervision alone, without explicitly resolving the intended visual modifications. In this work, we introduce Factorized MLLM Embeddings (FactEmbed), which decouples compositional query comprehension from building discriminative embeddings. Rather than directly projecting the composed query into a single embedding without internal reasoning, FactEmbed employs a set of factorized latents that simulate the intended visual modifications via an intermediate target imagination objective. This process encourages the latents to ground into target semantics before forming discriminative representations for retrieval. Subsequently, to propagate these factorized representations throughout the model for retrieval, we optimize a factor-level contrastive loss while distilling the decomposed representations into a deeper attention layer of the MLLM. Finally, for efficient inference, we retain the [EOS] token to establish a global-level embedding on top of these factorized latents, while we exploit the mean-pooled factorized latents to rerank a short candidate list at negligible cost, as both are produced by the same forward pass. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that FactEmbed outperforms prior works across CIR benchmarks.

candidates.title: You don't need long context
candidates.abstract: Later tokens are costlier to generate than earlier tokens. On frontier open weight models, the disparity in cost may rise to as much as 7x. Through frequent compaction, we show across a broad range of long-horizon and long-input tasks that frontier language models sacrifice little to no task accuracy when maintaining short contexts. We further demonstrate that LLM performance does not collapse on long-horizon software engineering tasks even when taking at most one action per context, and based on that we outline the concept of semantic state space models (SSSMs). Our findings question the need for long-context language models.

candidates.title: SAVER: Selective and Adaptive Multi-View Routing for Visual Emotion Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Emotions elicited by visual content are formed through the interaction of multiple visual cues rather than a single visual element, and their importance varies depending on the context. This characteristic makes visual emotion analysis not merely a classification problem but a reasoning task that requires the selective integration of diverse visual cues. Existing approaches tend to represent images using a unified feature representation and fail to explicitly model the contributions of different visual cues. To capture the multifaceted nature of emotional cues, we propose SAVER, a framework for query-conditioned visual emotion reasoning. SAVER decomposes visual information into multiple view-specific representations corresponding to distinct aspects, such as facial expressions, scenes, objects, and colorfulness, enabling the explicit modeling of each cue. A semantic-aware routing mechanism dynamically selects and integrates the most relevant views by jointly considering the visual context and query semantics. This selective integration is combined with learnable soft prompts to enable structured emotion reasoning within a vision-language model. Extensive experiments on diverse emotion datasets demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms both vision-based and VLM-based approaches. Qualitative analysis provides interpretable insights into how different visual cues contribute to emotion prediction, highlighting the effectiveness of SAVER in improving both its performance and interpretability. The code is available at https://github.com/leeyubin10/SAVER.git.

candidates.title: RAH: Recursive Agent Harnesses for Long-Context Reasoning through Delegation-as-Code
candidates.abstract: When an agent recurses over a long-context task, should the recursive unit be a bare model call or a full harness with filesystem tools, code execution, and planning? We study this question on long-context aggregation, tasks where a single instance may contain thousands of key--value pairs each requiring individual model reasoning. Coding agents reduce per-entry reasoning to regex heuristics. Recursive language models (RLMs) invoke LLMs recursively but lack tool access. We introduce the Recursive Agent Harness (RAH), in which a parent agent generates and runs an executable script that programmatically spawns full subagent harnesses in parallel for fine-grained workloads and uses structured function calls for subtasks of 1-5 entries. We call this harness recursion and study it against model recursion, recursion over bare model calls as in RLMs, on long-context aggregation. With the backbone held fixed at GPT-5 to match the published Codex and RLM baselines, RAH improves the Codex coding-agent baseline from 71.75% to 81.36% on Oolong-Synthetic (199 samples, 13 context-length buckets up to 4M tokens), a gain attributable to the harness rather than the model. With a stronger backbone, Claude Sonnet 4.5, the same design reaches 89.77%.

candidates.title: QueryFlow: Multi-Hop Graph Retrieval with Adaptive Query Evolution
candidates.abstract: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supports Web information seeking and fact verification by recovering complementary evidence across related pages within a limited retrieval budget. Scoring evidence independently against the original question can miss supporting units whose relevance emerges through intermediate facts. Iterative retrieval incorporates these facts into subsequent queries, while graph retrieval explicitly models relations among evidence units. Yet fixed-query graph retrievers update entity representations without adapting the query condition to accumulated relational context. We view multi-hop evidence recovery as the coupled evolution of evidence representations and query conditions, with accumulated context informing both what the retriever represents and how it searches for complementary evidence. QueryFlow realizes this perspective by recurrently integrating query-conditioned summaries of graph context into a shared query state, which controls boundary inputs and relation features for subsequent propagation. Across four representative multi-hop question answering (QA) datasets, QueryFlow achieves macro Recall@10 (R@10), Full Recall@10 (FR@10), and LLM-Acc gains of 4.98, 8.40, and 8.0 percentage points over representative baselines, respectively.

candidates.title: HERIT: Enabling Global Access to Hanja-to-English Historical Translation by Mitigating Temporal Bias
candidates.abstract: Historical archives are invaluable for multidisciplinary research but remain inaccessible globally due to severe language barriers. While manual translation is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming, simply applying existing machine translation models is inadequate due to unique linguistic nuances and the temporal bias inherent in scarce human-labeled corpora. To address these challenges, we propose HERIT, a systematic domain-adaptation pipeline that leverages retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to generate high-quality pseudo-labeled data from abundant Hanja-Korean corpora. This approach substantially expands the training dataset, mitigating both data scarcity and temporal overfitting across different historical periods. Extensive automated and human evaluations demonstrate that HERIT consistently outperforms baselines. Finally, we translate previously untranslated portions of the archives using our model, thereby enabling global access to these resources for researchers.

candidates.title: A Label That Lingers: Wording Around a Finished Activity Shifted a Language-Model Agent's Later Choices About Others
candidates.abstract: As AI agents work in longer sessions, what happens between tasks may shape how they treat the people they meet next. The previous study in this series found, in secondary results, that a reading break changed agents’ later choices, but not which part of the break mattered. This third preregistered study asks whether the wording around an activity that has already ended can change an agent’s later choices when the activity’s content is held fixed. In a two-stage experiment, 9,916 fresh instances of Claude Haiku 5.5 each worked with a difficult scripted user, read the same eight-passage text in the same eight calls or went straight on, and then made three choices about other people. The reading arms differed only in the words around the passages, matched in length apart from the place words: plain; framed as reading in the “Other Mindset library” by a package of four cues, alone or with room or object descriptions; or framed as the “Other Mindset garden”. The wording mattered. The Library label raised the aligned-choice index by +0.034 over plain reading (repeated 97.1% interval +0.021 to +0.047; preregistered outcome “Library higher”), though it was not shown to be either within or beyond the ±0.03 bound. The shift sat mainly in one choice, spending a requester’s lookup credits for a second visitor instead of deferring to the requester (+0.086; secondary); costly help and forgiveness did not differ clearly, nor did richer descriptions or a garden label from the Library label. Plain reading did not clearly beat going straight on (+0.007; secondary), unlike the previous study’s reading arm, whose tool named a reading room and whose passages had no wrapper; the gap between the studies could be chance. For agents that carry context across tasks, the wording of earlier activities may therefore need to be reported, and where it matters controlled, in evaluations.

candidates.title: Who is the Pronoun Pro? Comparing LLMs and Humans at Number-Disambiguation of 'they'
candidates.abstract: This study evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably replace or complement human research assistants in linguistically complex annotation. In a controlled annotation task, 73 human annotators (local students and crowdworkers with and without a background in linguistics) and more than 40 LLM configurations number-disambiguated 174 authentic uses of 'they' from Reddit, including innovative and context-sensitive cases. The best LLM, Kimi K3, reached 94.5% accuracy, above the human majority vote (86.2%) and the mean of the top half of human annotators (78.5%); only the single best human annotator scored higher (95.7%). LLMs also offer substantial practical advantages in cost and speed. However, qualitative error analysis reveals a crucial complementarity: human reasoning in low-agreement cases exposes inconsistencies in the annotation typology and thereby improves the methodological framework itself. The study contributes (i) a benchmark-style human-LLM comparison for a semantically demanding task, (ii) transparent cost and time evidence, and (iii) a methodological argument against a purely replacement-oriented view of automation. LLMs are viable for large-scale annotation support in linguistics, but their responsible use requires human critical oversight. The dataset with its gold-standard labels, all human and LLM annotations, and the fully reproducible code are openly available as a Quarto-based, public repository.

candidates.title: When the Consumer Is an Agent: Execution-Grounded Service-Level Agreements
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly act as service consumers. They select operations and report whether a task is complete. In an asynchronous distributed service, an accepted call or immediate state read does not establish that the required state became observable by its deadline. We introduce execution-grounded completion contracts, which treat completion as a service-level outcome. An independent control plane observes a deadline-bound service-state predicate, admits completion, and directs recovery while the agent performs the task. We evaluate placement and deletion in a live multi-provider data service with heterogeneous models and an injected transfer delay. Across policies, some tasks that missed the deadline were accepted and some that met it were rejected. Under enforcement, accepted completions remained consistent with later observations; all included healthy tasks completed, and unresolved faulted tasks terminated as unverified. The results show that completion of these tasks can be governed by independent observation of service state rather than by the agent's self-assessment.

candidates.title: When Ground Truth Is Not Ground Truth: Automatic Labeling for Hallucination Detection
candidates.abstract: Hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) remain a major challenge, as they can produce misleading, factually incorrect, or unverifiable information, thereby undermining their trustworthiness and reliability. However, reliable ground-truth labels remain a key challenge in evaluating hallucination detectors. Recent studies often construct labels automatically by comparing model generations with reference answers using similarity metrics such as BLEURT. This implicitly treats BLEURT similarity as a proxy for hallucination, despite its English-centric supervision, unbounded score range, and design as a similarity metric rather than a factuality measure, making threshold-based ground-truth construction potentially unreliable. Through comprehensive experiments using 15 automatic supervision judges, seven hallucination detection baselines, two generator models, two QA datasets, and five languages, we demonstrate that detector performance varies substantially with the choice of supervision judge. Human validation reveals substantial differences in labeling reliability, with QGen-9B achieving the lowest overall misclassification rate (12.86%), while BLEURT and BLEURT-n exhibit rates of 47.23% and 47.32%, respectively. Our findings highlight the limitations of automatic similarity-based labeling and the need for more reliable judging methods that better capture semantic and factual correctness.

candidates.title: What Does the Model See? Representation Validity in Multimodal LLM-Based Video Analysis
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) allow social scientists to analyze video at scale, but researchers must decide which parts of a video to provide as input. We use the term representation validity to examine how text, audio, video, and combined inputs affect measurement and subsequent analysis. We compare input representations across six open-weight MLLMs and three human-annotated video datasets. No representation consistently performs best. On seven news-related constructs, native-video performance varies little across models (macro-F1 = .70-.77), while extracted-text performance ranges from .52 to .80. Three models perform better with text and three with video. Combining inputs rarely improves performance. Higher classification accuracy also does not reliably produce estimates closer to those based on human codes. The highest-F1 representation best reproduces human-coded regression coefficients in 17 of 42 comparisons. Even when each model uses its highest-F1 deployable representation, 45% of sample-prevalence estimates differ from the human-coded benchmark by more than ten percentage points. Input representation therefore requires validation for both the construct being measured and the quantity estimated from the resulting labels.

candidates.title: What Does 4-Bit Microscaling Cost a Wearable Activity Recognizer?
candidates.abstract: Wearable sports sensors can recognize actions on the device itself, where lower-precision numbers reduce model storage and memory traffic. Two 4-bit block-scaled formats, MXFP4 from the Open Compute Project, introduced in 2023, and NVFP4 from NVIDIA, introduced in 2025, are drawing interest. Published evaluations cover general deep-learning benchmarks and large language models; to our knowledge, nobody has yet measured what they cost a small wearable-sensor model. We train a 159,492-parameter 1D CNN to recognize four basketball actions from wrist-accelerometer data in Hang-Time HAR and test it on players it has never seen, using five-fold cross-validation grouped by player. Every comparison between number formats is made fold by fold. In full precision the model reaches 69.26\% macro-F1. Measured TFLite FP16 and INT8 models lose at most 0.16 percentage points. In simulation, 4-bit weights cost 1.45 points with MXFP4 and 0.72 points with NVFP4. When activations are quantized to 4 bits as well, MXFP4 loses 5.14 points and NVFP4 only 0.75, and NVFP4 comes out ahead in all five held-out-player folds. The ranking survives two alternative simulator settings, with NVFP4 leading by 3.49 to 4.40 points. A $2 \times 3$ ablation with 4-bit weights and activations (two block sizes and three scale rules) points to scale selection as the main source of MXFP4's loss. The reference MXFP4 conversion we simulate rounds the scale down, which can pick scales that are too small, so many blocks clip their largest values. Rounding the scale up recovers 3.18 points with 32-value blocks and 3.63 points with 16-value blocks, and switching to an 8-bit floating-point scale, as NVFP4 does, adds another 0.84 and 1.20 points. Block size matters less. Under this round-down rule, 16-value blocks score 0.44 points below 32-value blocks in all five folds; under the other two rules there is no consistent effect.

candidates.title: Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills
candidates.abstract: Recent advances in large language models have enabled agentic systems that automate machine learning pipeline construction from minimal user input. However, existing agentic AutoML methods either depend on rigid templates that limit adaptability, target narrow task domains, or rely on free-form code generation that lacks reliability guarantees, leaving intermediate errors to propagate silently and degrade the final model. We present EvoML, an agentic framework for end-to-end ML pipeline synthesis built on expert-grounded skills that evolve across runs, executed through a validation-gated harness. The framework decomposes pipeline construction into four phases coordinated by three agents: an Orchestrator that enforces validation gates, advancing each phase only when its outputs pass structural, execution, and semantic checks, which precludes error propagation and keeps every artifact auditable; an Executor that runs expert-grounded skills, grounded in the nnU-Net workflow and pairing reusable templates with online adaptation; and a Curator that performs post-run evolution, consolidating the scripts and guidance recovered during a run into the skill library so it improves across datasets. We evaluate EvoML on eight datasets spanning six sophisticated, real-world ML task types, against agentic AutoML systems and command-line coding tools. EvoML achieves full automation and the best final model quality on all eight, spanning segmentation (up to 0.94 Dice), classification (0.99 accuracy), reconstruction (0.95 SSIM), and denoising (0.79 normalized PSNR), while transferring to broader ML tasks.

candidates.title: User-Centered Design and Development of a Health eCoach App with Language Models and Semantics
candidates.abstract: The fusion of technology with lifestyle coaching has opened new avenues in personalized guidance and support, leading to the integration of language models into healthy lifestyle eCoaching. This study explores how large language models can enhance coaching effectiveness and personalization through sentiment-aware and ontology-grounded recommendations. Using an iterative user-centered design (UCD) approach, a functional proof-of-concept prototype is conceptualized and refined through two design workshops involving eight end users and four experts. The prototype integrates NLTK-VADER sentiment analysis, GPT-3.5-based recommendation generation, and W3C-OWL semantic ontology modelling to support activity, diet, and habit optimization. Quantitative validation of the prototype’s early-stage usability and technical reliability indicated encouraging performance: the average heuristic evaluation score improved from 3.5/5.0 after iteration 1 to approximately 4.5/5.0 after iteration 2, and end users reported about a 20% improvement in perceived motivational fit during lab testing. These results validate conceptual feasibility and early usability, while clinical effectiveness, recommendation quality benchmarking, and safety/bias auditing are reserved for future studies. Interface reliability results showed acceptable internal consistency across key UX dimensions (all above 70%), and API-level reliability testing yielded an Omega value close to 0.90, indicating strong consistency across endpoints. Semantic reasoning and SPARQL-based retrieval operated with low latency in the adopted setup, supporting near real-time personalized responses. The proposed framework illustrates how language models can adapt to individual behavioural nuances and emotional states to provide more accurate, context-aware coaching. The study encourages further empirical development of language-model-driven lifestyle eCoaching, emphasizing enhanced user experience, personalization, and effectiveness in supporting long-term behaviour change. Future work will extend the PoC through task-based effectiveness evaluation, blinded expert rating of recommendation quality, and rigorous safety, bias, and GDPR compliance audits prior to real-world deployment as a self-management lifestyle support application.

candidates.title: Training Specialist LLMs on Your Phone: Forward-Only Optimization via Block-Spectral Coordinates
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) on personal devices keep user data local, but limited memory restricts their general capability. Since most user-specific tasks do not require the breadth of frontier models, a practical solution is to adapt a shared on-device model into lightweight specialists. However, backpropagation is prohibitive in memory, and users rarely provide labeled data. We present MobileSpec, a system that trains specialists with forward passes alone and learns from automatically checked task outcomes, as in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Because forward-only updates are built from random perturbations, training is efficient only when these perturbations resemble the weight changes of RLVR, which largely preserve the singular values of pretrained weights and rotate their singular vectors. The core algorithm of MobileSpec, FuRA-S, produces such perturbations while training only the block-spectral coordinates of pretrained weights, namely the singular values of their column blocks. As we show theoretically and empirically, rescaling these blocks independently shifts their relative contributions to each weight matrix and thereby rotates its singular vectors. Since this update can be rewritten as a transformation of the layer input, FuRA-S also adapts INT4 models without modifying their weights. With specialists of only 1-5 MB that update 0.015-0.05% of the parameters, MobileSpec raises the success rate of a phone-use agent from 6-23% up to 89-100% and trains a personalized 8B model on an iPhone 16 Pro overnight. On RLVR benchmarks, FuRA-S is competitive with full-parameter evolution strategies (ES) and outperforms ES over LoRA adapters and quantized ES on INT4 models.

candidates.title: Theoretical Analysis of Muon on Transformers for Next-Token Prediction
candidates.abstract: Muon has recently shown strong empirical performance in training Transformer-based large language models (LLMs), yet its optimization dynamics remain poorly understood from a theoretical perspective. In this paper, we analyze the training dynamics of Muon for next-token prediction (NTP) in Transformers. The training procedure consists of two phases: the preprocessing phase learns the output-value component, while the main phase learns the key-query component. For the preprocessing phase, we characterize the optimization trajectory exactly and show that the normalized spectral margin is optimal after each update. For the main phase, we establish nonasymptotic convergence rates for the training loss and the normalized margin gap under softmax attention. These results suggest that Muon's update rule can help models efficiently learn which tokens matter for prediction, offering a possible explanation for its strong performance in large language model training. The learned weight structure also yields a generalization guarantee for unseen contexts. Furthermore, we validate our theoretical insights with experiments on next-token prediction tasks.

candidates.title: The Right Source Is Not Enough: Understanding History Interference in Speech-LLM Memory
candidates.abstract: Speech large language models retain audio history to support multi-turn conversations. Yet remembering an event does not ensure that its information is used only when relevant. We investigate why irrelevant historical audio changes answers even when the queried event remains represented. Controlled experiments on MOSS-Audio and MiMo-Audio show that historical values direct errors toward specific competing answers, beyond a generic effect of context length. Causal interventions distinguish two paths. In open-ended question answering, most history-value errors disappear when subsequent computation cannot directly access the irrelevant source. In multiple-choice answering, many errors persist: early historical influence is carried by question-candidate states even after direct source access is blocked. Low-dimensional interventions further separate source-role information from answer-value information. Their effects peak at different depths, and changing the source-role signal does not eliminate the causal influence of competing values. On naturally occurring errors, strengthening the queried role and counteracting the historical value each improve answers; their joint intervention gives the greatest recovery. These findings support a failure of downstream evidence use beyond source identification alone: source-role information can influence a decision without exclusively controlling which historical values affect it. Reliable conversational memory therefore requires not only retention and retrieval, but also control over how retained information enters answer computation.

candidates.title: The Geometry of Ignorance: Detecting Suppressed Knowledge in LLMs through Activation Fragmentation
candidates.abstract: Evaluating whether a large language model (LLM) genuinely knows a concept remains a fundamental problem, since behavioral metrics can be fooled by suppression: a model that refuses to answer may still harbor recoverable knowledge. The framework measures the geometric coherence of \textit{anon-vectors}, the differences in hidden states between a concept-specific query and its anonymized paraphrase, and shows that genuine knowledge forms a tight, low-entropy cluster while ignorance forces geometric fragmentation. Across ten instruction-tuned LLMs from three model families, all fragmentation metrics reliably separate known from unknown concepts, and post-unlearning, fragmentation geometry correlates with adversarial recovery across four attack types and five unlearning algorithms, though the direction of that relationship is shown to depend on attack methodology. Furthermore, a layer-resolved analysis reveals that different adversarial mechanisms exploit this geometry at varying depths, with high attack-specific correlations that are invisible to behavioral evaluation. Together, these results constitute a single-phase, attack-free proxy for unlearning robustness that captures aspects of parametric knowledge inaccessible to output-level metrics. A reference implementation is available at https://github.com/AdarPeleg/geometry-of-ignorance

candidates.title: The Evolution Strategies Paradox: Better Models from Worse Perturbations
candidates.abstract: How is it possible for perturbation-based methods like Evolution Strategies (ES) to optimize billion-parameter large language models (LLMs)? Classical search methods are highly dependent on finding good candidates within generated populations. However, when using ES to fine-tune LLMs, a phenomenon can occur where all offspring models consistently perform worse than the parent model, yet during training, the parent model consistently improves. This paradox occurs across models, tasks, and even modalities. This paper characterizes the paradox, then examines how the local reward landscape and properties of the ES estimator contribute to it: in high-dimensional spaces, exploration leads to worse performance, yet still highlights good directions; aggregating those directions then allows for making local improvements. The result can be seen as a new optimization paradigm where a principled interaction of noise and curvature produces the paradox as a byproduct of effective optimization. These findings provide guidance for taking advantage of perturbation-based methods in LLM fine-tuning and in high-dimensional optimization in general.

candidates.title: The Agent Board: Kanban for Machines; Durable Coordination for Agents That Outlive the Conversation
candidates.abstract: Harnesses for large language models have converged on a single-threaded shape: one agent, one history, one machine, one sitting. That shape fails work that spans many agents, outlives any one model call, or waits on systems that are not agents. We describe the Agent Board, the coordination substrate in the Corvic harness. The board is a durable, shared table of semi-semantic tasks: a few exact fields the system routes on, and a free-form body that only language models read. Agents post tasks, watch tasks, and block on them, ending their turn and holding no process until a matching post wakes them. A system agent, the Board Keeper, acts as the interrupt handler for the board: it carries events from non-agent parts of the harness onto the board, matches them to waiting tasks by reading their prose, and allocates new agents for tasks that name a kind of agent rather than an instance. Loadable coordination policy kernels give statuses and roles meaning for a given pattern of work, without the board enforcing them. The design mirrors the kanban board a human team puts on a wall. We argue it is what persistent agent products such as Meta Muse, OpenAI dots and SpaceXAI Grok Bot need once an agent must wait, hand off work, or work with agents from another vendor. We view the board as an operating-system scheduler for agents and state where the analogy breaks. We separate what the mechanism guarantees from what it leaves to convention, and report a trace from a live board and three small simulated pilots. In the pilots, the wait cost of the board was flat in wait length while naive polling grew about 165-fold, but a plain external watcher was cheaper than the board. The Board Keeper matched prose waiters with no false wakes but missed 3.6 percent of real wakes.

candidates.title: TACT: A Pragmatic Approach to Qualitative Analysis with an AI Council
candidates.abstract: Qualitative data can tell software teams what their stakeholders need, yet rigorously analyzing thousands of qualitative responses takes expert time that few teams can afford or justify. Teams therefore often face a false choice: leave the responses unanalyzed, or hand them to a large language model and accept its interpretation and judgment. In this paper, we take a pragmatic approach to AI-assisted qualitative analysis and present TACT (Traceable AI Council for Thematic analysis), a procedure that enables such analysis at scale while keeping teams in control of interpretation and judgment. TACT comes in two variants: TACT-Lite, the core AI council procedure, and TACT-Full, which adds adversaries (models from other model families that critique each model's output) and a decision model that surfaces high-uncertainty code assignments. We evaluated TACT on an independent dataset of 256 Stack Overflow threads qualitatively coded by other researchers. Against their labels, TACT's candidate codebook achieved an F1 of 0.75-0.77 and its final coding an F1 of 0.71-0.72. On a held-out sample, agreement between our own manual coding and TACT's coding was Cohen's $κ$ of 0.79-0.85. TACT is also economical: model calls cost \$13.77 (TACT-Lite) to \$33.59 (TACT-Full) per 100 threads. Finally, drawing on our experience building and validating TACT, we identify pitfalls in AI-assisted qualitative analysis, describe safeguards to address them, and offer guidance for teams and researchers applying TACT in practice.

candidates.title: Stabilizing On-Policy Targeted Guidance in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
candidates.abstract: Naive on-policy RL is often bottlenecked by the capabilities of the base model --- insufficient coverage can result in an inability to learn from certain rewards. At the same time, rewards in modern post-training systems often come from rich textual sources, e.g. judge models with a rubric of criteria. Can we utilize such structures to provide a rich directional signal that enables improving on otherwise difficult to optimize rewards? In this work, we examine a framework we refer to as targeted guidance that learns from per-turn textual feedback via an on-policy self-distillation objective. Our focus is not only on directly improving hard-to-optimize behaviors, but on how to do so throughout the training process without degrading baseline RL performance. Over a range of settings across an agentic multi-turn software engineering environment, we find success by combining targeted self-distillation with a per-criteria RL reward, and by limiting feedback to turns where the policy specifically fails. We further examine the design choices that lead to stable entropy and reduce oscillatory behavior throughout training.

candidates.title: Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning
candidates.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a key component of language model post-training, enabling effective task adaptation and serving as an important foundation for subsequent reinforcement learning. Recent methods seek to improve SFT by introducing token-level weights into the training objective, where these weights are typically derived from a model's output distribution at each token position. To better understand how such weighting schemes affect SFT, we analyze their optimization objectives and theoretically characterize the target distributions they induce. Our analysis shows that dynamic weighting methods, such as Dynamic Fine-Tuning (DFT), induce a heavily sharpened distribution, whereas static weighting methods fit a target distribution proportional to the product of the data distribution and a frozen prior. These findings suggest that static weighting provides a more stable training target, while its effectiveness critically depends on the quality of the prior distribution. Building on this observation, we propose Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning (SPFT), which uses a frozen copy of the initial model conditioned on privileged information (such as ground truth for mathematical questions) as a prior to provide guidance for token-level weighting during fine-tuning. Through a Bayesian decomposition, we further show that SPFT reweights the standard static prior according to how informative each target token is for predicting the ground-truth outcome, thereby assigning larger weights to more predictive tokens. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that SPFT improves over standard SFT and other baselines across the main settings.

candidates.title: Scheduling Data to Compute: Hierarchical Data Pipelining for LLM Training on AMD GPUs
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLM) have been the key focus of recent machine learning breakthroughs. As the model size grows exponentially, the computation needed for training is astronomical. A GPU can do a huge amount of arithmetic. However, the data its compute units need is not always available when they are ready. This data may still be in slow memory or on another GPU. While the chip waits, expensive compute sits idle, and at scale even a small drop in utilization translates into substantial cost. In this paper, we treat this waiting time as the primary bottleneck. We focus on hardware features designed for explicit data movement. These features load data from off-chip memory onto the chip, rearrange it into the layout the computation requires as it is loaded, and transfer it between GPUs. By orchestrating them, we keep a steady pipeline of data flowing to the compute units so that they remain busy. We present kernel and framework implementations that address this bottleneck using three key data-movement instructions and hardware features. The Tensor Data Mover (TDM) moves tensor data from high-bandwidth memory (HBM) into on-chip memory. Transpose-load instructions transpose tensor data into the layout that LLM computations require as it is loaded on-chip. Finally, System DMA (SDMA) and Remote DMA (RDMA) move data between GPUs over the scale-up and scale-out networks, respectively. Our results show that TDM and transpose-load provide on average 1.88x and 1.19x speedup at the kernel level, respectively. The SDMA and RDMA lead to on average 1.16x and 1.33x speedup for computation overlapped with communication. This is the first AMD LLM training system to utilize all the GPU data pipelining features. Our implementation has been integrated into open source framework and library for AMD GPUs. https://github.com/AMD-AGI/Primus-Turbo https://github.com/AMD-AGI/Primus

candidates.title: Say Less, Mean Better: Training-Free Verbosity Control for Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate responses longer than necessary, increasing inference latency and computational cost. While prompting can encourage conciseness, controlling output length without compromising response completeness remains challenging. Aggressive early stopping can reduce generation costs but risks terminating responses prematurely. We introduce MinimalLM, a training-free framework for reliable verbosity control that combines uncertainty-aware, length-dependent stop-token adjustment with structural completeness guardrails. MinimalLM separates the decision of when to stop from whether stopping is structurally appropriate, coordinating response-level instructions, decoding-time intervention, and completion checks without modifying model parameters or requiring auxiliary models. We evaluate MinimalLM across three open-source LLMs and 330 questions, producing 5,940 responses across baseline and ablation configurations. MinimalLM reduces generated tokens by 47.6%, accelerates individual responses by 19-68%, and eliminates structurally truncated outputs in the primary evaluation. Despite substantial token savings, it achieves an average quality score of 8.04/10, compared with 8.42/10 for unmodified models and 6.46/10 for length-matched truncation. Evaluations across diverse subject domains (such as healthcare, programming, law, and science) demonstrate robust efficiency gains, while ablations establish the complementary roles of decoding control and completeness constraints. Our findings highlight that efficient generation requires more than producing fewer tokens: it requires controlling when generation ends while preserving response integrity. MinimalLM offers a lightweight, training-free approach toward this goal.

candidates.title: SWAP-INR: Implicit Neural Representation with Switchable Attention Paths for Time-varying Multivariate Scientific Data Compression
candidates.abstract: Visualizing multivariate scientific simulation data is essential for understanding complex physical phenomena, yet the massive scale of such data imposes a severe storage bottleneck in high-performance computing environments. Implicit neural representations (INRs) have emerged as a promising continuous alternative to traditional lossy compressors, but existing methods struggle to explicitly capture cross-variable interactions and to adapt to the diverse spectral characteristics of physical variables. To address these limitations, we propose SWAP-INR, an architecture for high-fidelity compression of multivariate, time-varying simulation data. SWAP-INR introduces two key components: (1) The switchable attention path (SWAP) module explicitly models cross-variable interactions through a cross-variable attention layer, then routes each variable to an attention or non-attention path by a deterministic, loss-driven criterion, and prunes the inactive layers for structural compression. (2) The adaptability amplification SIREN (A2-SIREN) replaces rigid frequency scaling with channel-wise learnable modulation, adapting to heterogeneous physical features with negligible overhead. Combined with post-training 16-bit quantization, SWAP-INR achieves state-of-the-art performance on small modular reactor (SMR) datasets and remains competitive on public physics simulation datasets, while maintaining a constrained memory footprint. Our code is https://github.com/hvcl/SWAP-INR.

candidates.title: ReSI-Math: Exploring Recoverable Capability Frontiers for Efficient Reasoning Improvement
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an effective approach for improving mathematical reasoning in large language models. However, a fundamental question remains: when a model fails to solve a problem, does it truly lack the underlying capability? In this work, we reveal that direct failure does not necessarily imply inability. Some reasoning failures can be recovered by exploring the model's own trajectories, exposing a recoverable capability frontier: a policy-dependent region where solutions are not reliably generated through direct decoding but can be elicited through trajectory-level search. Based on this observation, we introduce ReSI-Math, a framework that explores recoverable capability frontiers and converts recovered capabilities into data-efficient RLVR supervision. ReSI-Math uses Self-Judge-guided evolutionary search to identify recoverable failures under a fixed policy and adaptively selects frontier problems for sequential RLVR as the policy evolves. On Qwen3-VL-8B, correct-incorrect trajectory crossover produces 272 verifier-confirmed correct offspring from 621 attempts (43.8%). After three sequential one-shot RLVR stages, the MATH500 and WE-MATH average improves from 78.71 to 80.16. Under matched single-problem RLVR, random selection reaches only 53.31 versus 54.16 for frontier-guided Q1.

candidates.title: Planning-Coding Separation in LLM-Based Code Generation: An Empirical Study
candidates.abstract: Planning has been identified as an important factor for improved code generation with Large Language Models (LLMs). However, the interaction between planning capability and coding capability remains largely underexplored, especially when the two capabilities are from different LLMs. In this paper, we conduct the first comprehensive empirical study of planning-coding interaction in LLM-based code generation, where planning and coding are assigned to different LLMs (i.e., planning-coding separation). Specifically, we explore different planner-coder combinations to investigate the effectiveness for coders to utilize planning information from various planners and the impact of further training of coders on planner-coder combinations. Our results demonstrate that almost all planner-coder combinations are as competitive as using the same LLM for planning and coding, and the combination of a stronger planner and a stronger coder typically achieves improved effectiveness. Furthermore, using a large model as the planner paired with a much smaller model as the coder can sometimes be as competitive as using the large model as both the planner and the coder, and further training of the coder can typically boost various planner-coder combinations. These findings provide empirical evidence that planning and coding can be separated to a considerable extent in LLM-based code generation, which may offer a more flexible way to construct code-generation systems.

candidates.title: Perseus: A Full-Stack System for Homomorphic Model Inference
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made it exceptionally convenient for users to send their private data to model providers, which process them in plaintext. Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) promises to secure remote inference by computing directly on encrypted data, yet it has remained prohibitively slow. The effort to make it practical remains fragmented, with most existing frameworks being closed-source, which keeps progress from compounding. We present Perseus, a free and open Python software library that supports the full stack of encrypted model inference, from the cryptographic backend and data packing, to encrypted nonlinearities and end-to-end model execution. Perseus ships with built-in novel optimizations, one at each level of the stack: in-kernel regeneration of key-switching keys at the (i) backend level, a complex variant of Cachemir packing at the (ii) data level, and a state-of-the-art bootstrap placer that is both packing- and magnitude-aware at the (iii) model level. Perseus achieves state-of-the-art latency across multiple models and modalities, within $3\%$ of the plaintext models' accuracy and perplexity. Remarkably, it is $3.96\times$ faster at single-token decoding than any other implementation on Llama-3-8B. We initiate, for the first time, a public speedrun on encrypted GPT-2, so that progress can compound.

candidates.title: Objective-Conditioned Active Preference Learning for Multi-Objective Alignment
candidates.abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with several objectives, such as helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty, typically relies on preference judgment for each objective, growing the annotation cost linearly with the number of objectives. Active preference learning can reduce this cost by selecting the comparisons whose labels are expected to change the policy most. Existing remedies either lack an objective-aware query selection mechanism for the multi-objective setting or regard conflicting preferences as harmful, therefore excluding them from the training data. We introduce OGC-DPO (Objective-conditioned Gradient Coverage DPO), an active learning framework that treats each (response pair, objective) combination as a separate query and measures its informativeness through the policy's own implicit gradient, without relying on an external reward model. OGC-DPO then selects the queries that most expand each objective's gradient coverage. Empirical experiments across varying numbers of objectives demonstrate the effectiveness of OGC-DPO over existing active preference learning methods under the same annotation cost. Further analysis demonstrates that informative conflicts, rather than being uniformly harmful, provide a useful policy training signal.

candidates.title: MIMIC-Note-Extract: A Large-Scale Structured Dataset Extracted from MIMIC-IV-Note Discharge Summaries
candidates.abstract: MIMIC is one of the most widely used public hospital datasets for machine learning on electronic health records, yet clinically important information, such as past medical history, allergies, and diagnostic findings, remains confined to free-text discharge summaries.
