candidates.title: INSTRUCTION ARCHITECTURE IN GENERATIVE AI: A FRAMEWORK FOR PROMPT ENGINEERING AND REASONING CONTROL IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
candidates.abstract: The rapid use of large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek, Perplexity, Elicit, and others, has transformed human-computer interaction by prioritizing natural language processing over conventional programming methods. The introduced paradigm change emphasizes the essential talent of rapid production, which can determine the correctness, reliability, inventiveness, and safety of AI outputs. It is now a matter of introducing prompt engineering as a methodological field and its significance in practical implementation in various disciplines of research, education, and decision-making. Despite its extensive utilization, the evolution of instant invention has been inadequately organized, sometimes regarded as an ad hoc or intuitive process. The article provides a comprehensive, methodical, and pragmatic examination of prompt creation, integrating theoretical foundations of contemporary AI architectures with practical prompting strategies. It entails the assessment of architectural, cognitive, and probabilistic concepts underlying contemporary AI systems. The taxonomy of prompts, design methodology, optimization, and evaluation methodologies is applied to real-world scenarios in research, software engineering, education, and decision-making. The monograph aims to establish immediate invention as a methodological discipline, contrasting it with an undisciplined creative form.

candidates.title: Correctness and Completeness of a Multimodal Large Language Model in the Diagnosis and Treatment Recommendations for Proximal Femoral Fractures
candidates.abstract: Background and Objectives: To compare the diagnostic and therapeutic performance of a multimodal large language model (GPT) with that of two human evaluators in proximal femoral fracture (PFF) assessment, focusing on correctness and completeness. Materials and Methods: A consecutive series of 250 PFFs was reconstructed into standardized clinical scenarios including radiographs and structured clinical data. Each case was independently evaluated by a trauma fellow, a second-year orthopaedic resident, and GPT. Responses were scored for diagnostic and treatment correctness and completeness. Severe treatment errors were predefined as category-changing mismatches, failure to recognize an existing implant, or incorrect laterality. Results: Fully correct diagnoses were achieved in 97.2% of cases by the fellow, 44.8% by the resident, and 14.0% by GPT (p < 0.001). GPT showed lower odds of correct diagnosis compared with the resident (matched OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.14–0.37) and fellow (OR 0.005, 95% CI 0.0001–0.03), with clustering of errors in extracapsular fractures. Diagnostic completeness also differed significantly (p < 0.001), with GPT providing fully complete assessments in 60.4% of the cases (151/250). Fully correct treatment recommendations were provided in 98.8%, 81.2%, and 36.4% of cases, respectively (p < 0.001). Severe treatment errors occurred in 58.8% of GPT outputs versus 2.0% and 0% for the resident and fellow (OR vs. resident 36.5, 95% CI 13.95–135.75). Although treatment completeness was high (93.2%), 58.8% (147/250) of GPT responses were complete but incorrect. Conclusions: GPT demonstrated substantial limitations in both diagnostic and therapeutic reasoning for PFF, with frequent pattern-dependent errors and a high rate of clinically consequential treatment mismatches.

candidates.title: AI-Based Multimodal Phishing Detection Using Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Phishing is one of the most common cybersecurity threats where attackers trick users through fake emails, websites, or links to steal sensitive information. With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, phishing attacks are becoming more realistic and harder to detect using traditional methods. Earlier systems relied on blacklists, rules, and URL features, but recent research explores deep learning, Large Language Models (LLMs), and multimodal approaches. Explainability and privacy-aware techniques such as federated learning are also gaining importance. The increasing sophistication of phishing campaigns highlights the need for advanced detection frameworks that can analyze diverse information sources simultaneously. Mul-timodal systems leverage text, URLs, visual webpage content, and embedded scripts to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of suspicious activity. Large Language Mod-els further enhance semantic understanding, enabling detection of subtle manipulations in phishing messages. By combining multimodal analysis with explainable and privacy-preserving AI, researchers aim to build adaptive, transparent, and trustworthy solutions that can effectively counter evolving phishing threats in real-world cybersecurity environ-ments.

candidates.title: ASCENT: Scale-complementary external state for frozen long-context language models
candidates.abstract: External state should become more valuable as a reader becomes more capable, yet long-context evaluations measure memory utility at a single model scale. This paper formulates scale complementarity: the absolute gain from external state increases when reader capacity and a compact state budget are jointly scaled. ASCENT realizes this principle with a target-blind causal writer, nested typed state, and a bounded query-conditioned readout; every language model remains frozen. Under log loss, the value of a nested refinement equals its target-relevant conditional information; a full factorial makes the reader-by-state interaction identifiable. Official 16 K BABILong experiments show Qwen2.5 accuracy gains of 10.50, 78.88, and 82.63 percentage points at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters, with both adjacent directional contrasts significant after family-wise correction. At 7B, Foundation accuracy rises to 33.25% while four-slot ASCENT answers every question, which caps the gain at 66.75 points; the 3B-to-7B accuracy increment is −15.88 points [−20.55, −11.20]. The accuracy-side claim is therefore established from 0.5B to 3B; the 7B conclusion rests on the non-saturated negative-log-likelihood factorial. A three-model by three-state factorial yields co-scaled negative log-likelihood gains of 0.388, 2.099, and 7.406 nats at 1.5B, 3B, and 7B; all interaction and gain contrasts retain positive simultaneous lower bounds. Five public 7B–8B readers obtain 66.75–85.63 point gains, and ASCENT exceeds task-trained retrieval checkpoints at the two larger shared scales. Controls, baselines, systems accounting, matched-hardware reproduction, and a cross-architecture sensitivity analysis accompany the experiments. The results establish scale-complementary external state under the evaluated benchmarks, metrics, and state schema.

candidates.title: Precision--Recall Trade-off on the Inference Level for LLMs in Grammatical Error Correction
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently been adopted for Grammatical Error Correction (GEC), achieving strong performance via both full fine-tuning and prompt-based approaches. As probabilistic sequence models, LLMs expose inference-time parameters that directly modify token generation behavior; however, their potential for controlling GEC-specific trade-offs has not been systematically studied. In this work, we investigate decoding strategies for grammatical error correction. We show that the repetition penalty parameter enables controllable adjustment of the precision--recall trade-off at inference time, without modifying the model architecture, training procedure, or prompt. Through experiments on standard GEC benchmarks, we demonstrate that repetition-penalty-based decoding enables inference-time control of the precision--recall balance, conceptually related to methods previously proposed for sequence-to-sequence GEC models, such as Align-and-Predict Decoding (APD), while remaining simple and broadly applicable to existing LLMs that expose inference-time decoding penalties.

candidates.title: Does Reasoning Make Language Models Agree?
candidates.abstract: Language models face two opposing concerns: monoculture, in which models err in correlated ways, and multiplicity, in which equally accurate models make conflicting decisions. The rise of reasoning models has complicated this debate: On the one hand, reasoning may increase model agreement if models anchor on the same salient features or follow similar reasoning paths. On the other hand, stochastic reasoning traces may introduce additional branch points leading to more diverse predictions. We resolve this tension by distinguishing reasoning as an intervention from reasoning as an observed behavior. We compare agreement under controlled changes in reasoning effort with agreement across observed reasoning lengths, measuring both against the agreement expected from model accuracy. Across nine models from two developers and three classification tasks, enabling reasoning increases agreement between models evaluated on the same individuals. Yet the individuals who elicit longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models. Both patterns persist after accounting for differences in accuracy. Asking models to reason more thus promotes agreement, while observing them reason longer signals disagreement.

candidates.title: Incentivizing Self-Learning in Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) draw on parametric knowledge and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to solve knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet problem solving in unfamiliar domains calls for tightly coupled knowledge acquisition and reasoning, beyond factual retrieval and aggregation or learning solely from a preassembled context. We study self-learning -- autonomously retrieving, studying, and applying knowledge from long-form reference materials on the fly. To investigate this capability, we formulate a textbook-based mathematical problem-solving task. LLMs must navigate textbook exposition, learn and apply relevant principles, and construct proofs for exercises, with reference solutions withheld. We introduce a BookNavigator interface to support this human-inspired study process and incentivize self-learning through reinforcement learning (RL) with fine-grained rewards. Experiments show that our method improves performance across in-domain and out-of-domain textbooks and subjects, raising Intern-S2-Preview-35B's overall proof accuracy from 51.5% to 79.5% and outperforming RL-trained textbook-free and fixed-retrieval baselines. These gains extend to complex long-context benchmarks involving different task types, with improvements over the base model of 1.7 and 2.3 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus and CL-bench, respectively. Together, these findings suggest that RL can foster a domain-agnostic self-learning strategy, highlighting the potential of self-learning from long-form corpora to strengthen broader problem-solving capabilities on complex, long-context tasks.

candidates.title: CaPtain: A Pipeline for Post-Training Code-as-Policy Robot Agents
candidates.abstract: Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it. Code-as-policy (CaP) casts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply. Yet existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware. We first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, then apply multi-turn RL. Multi-turn RL must credit tens of agent requests, whose physical effects often surface turns later, from a single end-of-episode outcome. We therefore introduce a physical critic that reads privileged simulator state, never seen by the policy, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success. Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B reaches 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points). Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation. We release all code, data, and model weights.

candidates.title: A Unified Hessian-Guided Framework for Post-Training Quantization
candidates.abstract: Low-bit quantization enables efficient deployment of large language models by reducing memory footprint and computational cost. Achieving high accuracy at low precision requires selecting quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding decisions. Existing approaches typically optimize these components independently using local reconstruction objectives, which fail to account for the varying impact of quantization errors on downstream predictions. Direct optimization of task-level metrics would provide a more faithful objective, but is challenging due to the discontinuous nature of quantization operations and the high computational cost of evaluating their downstream effects. In this work, we derive a Hessian-guided approximation of the output change induced by joint weight and activation quantization. Based on a tractable Fisher approximation, we formulate a unified post-training quantization framework that enables the joint optimization of quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding under a common output-sensitivity objective. The resulting method remains practical for modern large language models and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art transformation and rounding methods across both channel-wise and block-wise quantization settings.

candidates.title: Where Do Vision Language Models Fail at 3D Reasoning?
candidates.abstract: Vision-language models can get individual judgments right while struggling to recover and consistently use the exact properties of a 3D object. To characterize this gap, we introduce BedBench, a controlled benchmark of thirteen procedurally generated tasks spanning individual judgments and composite answers. Across twelve open-weight and four frontier models, per-color counting exposes a pronounced weakness: humans achieve 93.3% accuracy, compared with 7.2% for the best model. Targeted fine-tuning raises one model's accuracy from 3.0% to 68.6%, but reveals a further difficulty: its answers about the most common colors remain inconsistent with its own per-color counts. Supplying those counts as text improves its judgments, showing that recovering a property does not mean using it consistently. Reasoning, scaling, and added visual cues each improve individual judgments, but none makes exact answers reliable. To locate the difficulty, we probe Qwen3.5-27B: exact per-color counts remain recoverable at the language model's input, yet the model's answers rarely recover them (65.0% for the probe vs. 3.0% for the model). Image-removal controls further show that some apparent successes require no visual evidence. These findings motivate evaluating 3D reasoning by exact correctness, consistent use, and image dependence, rather than accuracy alone. Code and dataset are publicly available: https://github.com/leduckhai/BedBench

candidates.title: Turing LLM Post-Training: Calibrated Distillation and Efficient Dynamic-MoE Execution
candidates.abstract: We study post-training for dynamically routed mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, focusing on integrating independently optimized specialists while keeping consolidation efficient. Our approach combines calibrated multi-teacher on-policy distillation (C-MOPD), which matches each selected teacher on a local Top-$K$ support with teacher-wise loss normalization and clipping, with an execution path that uses post-capacity bounded-width dispatch, final-route replay, and asynchronous rollout--training overlap. On Turing-20B-A2B, the selected model achieves a four-domain normalized integration score of 0.9988 and retains at least 90.16\% of the measured specialist gain in every domain. At matched $K=32$, the full calibration objective scores 0.9962, compared with 0.9724 without calibration and 0.9834 without clipping. At a matched 8K response cap, the model exceeds both shared SFT and Qwen3-8B on all four reasoning-enabled mathematics and code benchmarks (unweighted mean: 85.92, versus 80.33 for Qwen3-8B and 74.21 for SFT), and improves over SFT on ten of twelve broader evaluation metrics. In a PPU-based profile, the combined execution configuration reduces consolidation step time from 398.7 to 139.3 seconds, an observed 2.86$\times$ speedup over serial execution. These results demonstrate strong specialist integration alongside more efficient consolidation, while reflecting the complete training and execution framework rather than any single component.

candidates.title: The psychophysics of affect in large language models
candidates.abstract: Good decisions often require considering how outcomes will feel. Yet large language models (LLMs) increasingly enter decision workflows, despite little being known about how they map outcomes to feelings or use those mappings in choice. We tested how LLMs anticipated gambling or stock-trading outcomes would feel and whether they incorporated these ratings into choice. When outcomes were rated in isolation, ratings exhibited diminishing sensitivity to magnitude, resembling human value functions; but models rated gains more intensely than equivalent losses, an inversion of canonical loss aversion we call silicon gain amplification. When outcomes were rated together, enabling direct comparison, ratings linearised. In choice, the gain-loss asymmetry largely disappeared, and models' own ratings did not reliably explain their choices better than monetary utility did. These findings reveal malleable mappings from outcomes to affect, raising questions about whether and how agentic LLMs should incorporate anticipated feelings into decisions.

candidates.title: Reasoning or Pattern Exploitation? Mechanistic Insights from RL-Trained Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly described as acquiring "reasoning" skills after reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. However, whether these gains reflect genuine reasoning or more superficial adaptations remains underexplored. In this work, we probe LLMs trained in a finite and exhaustively analyzable logical domain, namely Tic-Tac-Toe, and trace how internal representations evolve across reinforcement learning (RL) with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Quantitatively, RL yields high accuracy and robustness across prompt variations, suggesting the emergence of game reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability, however, paints a different picture: features extracted with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) reveal that models primarily adapt to rely more heavily on information already explicit in the prompt, such as whose turn it is, game progression and board occupancy. In comparison, high-level concepts like board symmetries and strategic forks remain weakly represented, raising concerns that reasoning benchmarks overestimate model abilities. This suggests that RL-driven "reasoning" may conflate task-specific adaptations to input information with reasoning ability. We provide, for the first time: (i) a systematic interpretability pipeline tracing representation dynamics across RL training in small-scale LLMs; (ii) an extension of SAE-based feature discovery to hypothesis-driven testing in a finite logical domain; and (iii) an interpretability-based demonstration that RL post-training neither adds nor removes concept information but reorganizes which features dominate the representation, with causal interventions locating the decision downstream of it, in the late-layer state.

candidates.title: Provenance-Aware PCR6 for Conflicting Evidence in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must often combine passages that are ambiguous, redundant, or mutually contradictory. This study asks whether proportional conflict redistribution from the Dezert-Smarandache theory (DSmT) provides a measurable advantage over Dempster-Shafer (DS) combination when both rules receive the same evidence and the same control for source dependence. Eight fusion methods were evaluated on 500 RAMDocs (Retrieval with Ambiguity and Misinformation in Documents) questions in three conditions. Under duplicated misinformation, provenance-aware PCR6 (Proportional Conflict Redistribution rule #6) reached 80.6% exact-set accuracy and 92.31% set F1, against 78.2% and 90.98% for provenance-matched DS; the exact-set difference was 2.4 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval [1.2, 3.8]) and the F1 difference was 1.33 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval [0.60, 2.33]). With NLI (natural language inference)-derived masses, PCR6 and DS selected identical answer sets, but PCR6 reduced Brier error. A preregistered 1,000-item multi-source experiment using singletons, proper unions, and total ignorance was followed by external validation on 428 RAMDocs items. In controlled partial-ignorance conflict, PCR6+ reduced BetP (betting probability transformation) Brier error from 0.3185 for PCR6 to 0.2733 and remained exactly neutral to an added vacuous BBA (basic belief assignment), although the DS rule achieved the lowest BetP Brier error of the three rules in that same controlled evaluation (0.1878). On the prespecified 260-item RAMDocs applicability subset, ordinary PCR6 had lower BetP Brier error than PCR6+ (0.2354 versus 0.2629), while both achieved set F1 = 0.7718. Exploratory decision sensitivity showed that maximum belief gave PCR6+ its best hard-decision result (exact set 0.5077; set F1 0.7859), whereas DSmP (Dezert-Smarandache probability transformation) sharpened rankings but worsened the RAMDocs Brier score. The evidence therefore supports a bounded claim: PCR6+ corrects a structural multi-source weakness of PCR6 under broad or vacuous focal evidence, but the best fusion and decision rules depend on the downstream loss and the mapping from text to BBAs.

candidates.title: Pegi1727/Quantifying-Fragility-of-Reasoning-in-LLMs-Replication-Package-: Replication Package and Empirical Datasets for: Quantifying the Fragility of Reasoning in Successive Generations of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: This repository contains the complete replication package, empirical datasets, analysis scripts, and high-resolution figures for the research study titled "Quantifying the Fragility of Reasoning in Successive Generations of Large Language Models". Overview & Framework Components Reasoning Predictive Equity (RPE): A metric tracking semantic fidelity via SBERT (all-mpnet-base-v2, cosine similarity scaled to [0,1]) against reference trajectories. Fragility Coefficient ($\lambda$): Parameter tracking exponential decay rate over successive generations ($RPE(g) = RPE_0 \cdot e^{-\lambda g}$). Critical Stability Horizon ($g^$): Threshold defined as 50% loss of semantic alignment ($g^ = \frac{\ln(2)}{\lambda}$). Repository Structure /data/: Empirical CSV datasets, Bayesian HDI fragility records, raw-like checks, and reconstructed parameter tables. /figures/: High-resolution publication-ready figures (300 DPI) including RPE trajectories, stability horizon bar charts, parameter comparisons, and the graphical abstract. /scripts/: Jupyter notebooks and Python scripts reproducing all statistical fits, analyses, and visualizations. /paper/: Compressed draft and manuscript documentation. candidates.title: MLLM-GS: Multimodal Large Language Model Prior-Guided Fast Novel View Synthesis in Extreme Environments
candidates.abstract: Novel view synthesis (NVS) in degraded scenes aims to reconstruct 3D scenes from multi-view observations affected by various degradations, and to generate clear and photorealistic images at unseen viewpoints. Despite recent advances, existing methods often rely on degradation-specific models, limiting their generalization across diverse extreme environments. Generative models provide rich visual priors, but their outputs often suffer from pixel misalignment and color deviations, which can propagate into the reconstructed 3D scene and compromise reconstruction quality. Furthermore, the high computational and memory costs of 3D reconstruction hinder the practical application of NVS in extreme environments. To this end, we propose MLLM-GS, a multimodal large language model (MLLM) prior-guided framework for fast NVS in extreme environments. MLLM-GS consists of two branches: MLLM prior-guided view enhancement and fast 3D scene reconstruction. The former leverages the rich visual priors of a frozen MLLM to enhance views under different severe degradations and introduces a lightweight correction network to reduce pixel shifts and color distortions in MLLM outputs. With supervision from only a few paired clean views, this branch produces reliable enhanced views for all degraded observations, providing pseudo-GT views for subsequent 3D reconstruction. The latter improves 3DGS efficiency by optimizing rasterization, Gaussian memory layout, and parameter updates, reducing redundant computation, memory-access overhead, and optimization costs. Extensive experiments on multiple degraded scenes demonstrate that MLLM-GS effectively handles various severe degradations and achieves high-quality NVS with significantly lower reconstruction time and memory consumption. candidates.title: LaplaceReason: A Certified Benchmark and Continuous Dynamic Systems Reasoning Suite for Frontier Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Abstract: Frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) such as DeepSeek-R1, OpenAI o1/o3, and Qwen-2.5-Math have achieved near-human proficiency on discrete reasoning benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, MATH). However, they systematically exhibit catastrophic hallucination, severe phase lag, and structural divergence when evaluated on continuous dynamic systems, multiscale stiff ordinary differential equations (ODEs), and high-order operational calculus. Traditional synthetic data pipelines fail to provide reliable supervision for these domains because conventional computer algebra solvers suffer from Wilkinson's catastrophic conditioning when factorizing high-order characteristic polynomials (K > 18). In this work, we present LaplaceReason, the first certified, massive reasoning benchmark designed to evaluate and train frontier LLMs on continuous multi-physics and dynamic systems. Ground truth solutions and step-by-step reasoning trajectories are certified via a deterministic, high-precision operational oracle guaranteeing machine-precision residual bounds (||R||_inf < 10^-14) across arbitrary orders without numerical root-finding. The benchmark spans seven fundamental task families:1. High-order rational dynamics (K from 2 to 60)2. Multiscale stiff ODEs (stiffness ratio S > 100x)3. Real-time randomized SVD with universal Gavish-Donoho noise rank thresholding4. 3D tomographic C-scan reconstruction5. Sub-millisecond zero-lag kinematic trajectory extrapolation6. Matrix-pencil modal extraction without Fourier spectral leakage7. Cascaded passive RLC ladder networks Deterministic Reinforcement Learning Verifier:The package provides an exact, rule-based reward model (laplace_cot_verifier) offering zero-inference-cost reward modeling for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). candidates.title: Incongruence-Aware Evaluation of Multimodal Speech Emotion Recognition in Audio Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Voice-interactive large language models process both what a speaker says and how they say it, yet the two channels do not always agree. We ask whether that disagreement degrades speech emotion recognition. Mapping text and audio into a shared valence-arousal-dominance space, we convert the distance between them into a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score with a two-component Gaussian mixture, and validate the score against human judgement. We evaluate three audiocapable models on acted, conversational and spontaneous speech (eNTERFACE'05, MELD and CMU-MOSEI). With the model held constant across modalities, incongruence raises the odds of error whenever audio is present, in every corpus, after controlling for the ground-truth emotion and for distance in the feature space. Supervised classifiers trained on the same features behave in the opposite way, which suggests that the difficulty lies in how these models combine raw evidence rather than in the signal itself. Text-only effects are unreliable: swapping only the model that reads the transcript reverses their sign on one corpus. Rebuilding the score without the emotion lexicon reproduces the central result, and among six simpler alternatives it is the only label-free score that predicts error in all three corpora. Code, data tables and prompts are released.

candidates.title: Category-Anchored Large Language Models for Next POI Recommendation
candidates.abstract: Next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation aims to predict a user's next destination from spatio-temporal check-in data, and serves as the foundation for many location-based services. Recent advances incorporate large language models (LLMs) into this task by textualizing user trajectories to exploit their semantic reasoning ability. However, directly generating POI identifiers with such models is unreliable: POIs are sparse, localized, and long-tailed entities with weak natural-language semantics, which creates a semantic-to-entity gap between high-level mobility intent and concrete POI prediction. To bridge this gap, we propose ANCHOR, a category-anchored framework for semantic-to-entity grounding in next POI recommendation. Specifically, ANCHOR first estimates category-level mobility intent in a compact and stable semantic space, rather than predicting concrete POI entities directly. The inferred intent is then grounded into a candidate set by integrating three complementary sources of mobility evidence: category anchors, historical visit memory, and user preferences. Finally, a history-aware reranker selects the target POI by matching each candidate with the user's historical mobility patterns and current context. Experiments on three real-world check-in datasets show that ANCHOR consistently outperforms representative traditional, structure-enhanced, and LLM-based baselines on the reported metrics. Further analyses validate the effectiveness of semantic-to-entity grounding and show favorable trade-offs among candidate coverage, ranking quality, and inference efficiency.

candidates.title: An evaluation of large language models for panoramic radiographs
candidates.abstract: Conversational multimodal models have demonstrated the ability to interpret medical images directly, but their performance on panoramic radiographs has not been systematically evaluated against dental reference standards. We systematically evaluated their ability to identify radiographic findings and localise the affected teeth. Reference labels were established by two experienced dentists, with disagreements resolved by consensus and, when necessary, adjudicated by a senior dentist. We evaluated seven models under zero-shot and four-shot conditions, with three runs per condition. We assessed seven binary tasks and three FDI localisation tasks using macro-averaged accuracy, valid-response rate, conditional F1, and FDI F1, and reported sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value with 95% confidence intervals. The GPT-5.4 family achieved the strongest overall image-level performance, although the leading model varied by task and prompting condition. GPT-5.4-mini achieved the highest four-shot FDI F1. Zero-shot macro-averaged accuracy was highest for GPT-5.4-mini (0.774), and four-shot accuracy was highest for GPT-5.4 (0.778). Compared with zero-shot prompting, four-shot prompting increased macro-averaged accuracy in six of seven models, with a maximum gain of 25.0 percentage points; GPT-5.4-mini decreased by 2.9 percentage points. GLM-4.6V-Flash had the largest increase, accompanied by a 0.383 increase in valid-response rate but a 0.122 decrease in conditional F1. Conditional F1 decreased in six models, and no condition had mean FDI F1 above 0.185. Four-shot prompting improved image-level accuracy in most models, but tooth-level localisation remained poor. This benchmark shows that improved image-level accuracy with four-shot prompting does not ensure reliable tooth-level localisation.

candidates.title: Attention, Dynamic Wave and Hybrid Sequence Mixers in Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on Multi-Head Attention (MHA) for sequence modeling, but scaling to long contexts is constrained by the quadratic cost of attention, motivating sub-quadratic recurrent alternatives. This paper formalizes a Dynamic Wave recurrent layer, based on input-dependent exponential damping and cosine phase modulation, and evaluates three 10.94M-parameter configurations (Pure Transformer, Pure Wave, and Hybrid Wave-Attention) on TinyStories under perplexity, latency, throughput and peak VRAM profiling up to 4096 tokens. The Hybrid configuration reaches the best perplexity, 5.95 on the full held-out split against 6.93 for the Transformer and 7.26 for Pure Wave. The efficiency picture, however, is governed by implementation rather than by architecture. Against an unfused attention baseline, Pure Wave uses 78.7% less peak VRAM at a 4096-token context (1404.3 MB vs. 6601.6 MB); against a fused scaled-dot-product attention kernel the same comparison yields no advantage at all (1404.3 MB vs. 1403.6 MB), and in training mode Pure Wave is 8.3% more expensive than the Transformer. Likewise, hoisting elementwise terms out of the recurrence loop speeds the layer up 2.53-fold with no custom kernel, reducing its latency gap to attention from 2.48-fold to 1.12-fold. A hybrid stack is found to inherit the cost of its more expensive mixer rather than the advantage of its cheaper one, its peak VRAM matching the Pure Transformer to within 0.1%. A closed-form memory model reproduces these measurements and predicts the context length beyond which attention overtakes the vocabulary projection. The findings indicate that reported efficiency gains for recurrent attention replacements must be stated relative to a named attention backend and a named implementation, and that hybridization is best justified on quality grounds.

candidates.title: On the Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning
candidates.abstract: On-policy reinforcement learning for large language models assumes that training responses are sampled from the current policy. In practice, an inference engine samples the responses and a separate trainer computes the gradients, and the \textbf{training-inference mismatch} between the two makes the training data off-policy. The mismatch has two sources, the numerics of the engine and the stale weights of asynchronous sampling, and a correction that stabilizes training under one source can fail under the other. \textit{We ask which property of a mismatch source decides the correction it needs.} Evaluating the trainer at the sampler's weights splits each sampled-token error exactly into a \textit{numerical discrepancy} of the engine and a \textit{policy lag} of the trainer, and we follow both through training. The numerical discrepancy stays approximately constant, so it biases the updates by a nearly fixed amount, and centering the score at each prefix removes its leading bias. The policy lag is produced by the trainer's own updates: the bias it leaves enters the next update, which enlarges the next lag and closes a feedback loop. Importance weighting cuts this loop only while the lag ratio stays concentrated, and on Qwen3-1.7B it fails at the step where the effective sample size of the ratio falls below one half. From this account we derive the \textbf{discrepancy-lag correction} (DLC), which centers the numerical discrepancy, clips the lag ratio against the sampler's weights and resynchronizes the sampler when this effective sample size falls below one half. Under a stale sampler, DLC keeps the KL divergence from on-policy training within twice the KL between two independent on-policy trainings on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, and its resynchronization prevents collapses that the per-token corrections leave and that a KL measured on the sampler's prefixes does not detect.

candidates.title: DolphinRouting: Cluster-Level Binary Routing for Disaggregated LLM Inference Serving
candidates.abstract: Prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation isolates the two phases of large language model serving, but request-level path selection must account for prefill work, cache reuse, and decode demand. We present DolphinRouting, which learns this choice from end-to-end SLO feedback under a given P/D resource allocation. Requests are clustered by raw prompt length, cache-adjusted input lengths on both worker pools, and output-length information. Offline policy search learns one binary action per cluster. Online feature extraction, cluster assignment, and table lookup select local or remote prefill. We evaluate DolphinRouting on a real PD-disaggregated cluster using three public benchmarks, a mixed workload, and real data. Across the mixed workload and real data, DolphinRouting with $k$-means reduces P90 TTFT by 5.7--7.9\% and P90 TPOT by 2.6--10.1\% relative to Dynamo.

candidates.title: Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) treat all context tokens uniformly, lacking explicit separation between executable instructions and passive data. This leads to prompt injection vulnerabilities, ambiguous instruction binding, and unreliable execution control. We present a post-training methodology using LLMON (LLM Object Notation), a framework that enables separating instructions from data and requires explicit identifier-based execution. We construct a large-scale structured training corpus of 4.6B tokens spanning general, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), and tool-calling data, augmented with distractor-infused variants in which competing instructions and irrelevant data segments are present in context but not referenced. Post-training two Granite-4.1 base models (3B and 8B) through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, we show that LLMON-structured supervision reduces attack success rates on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53-100% to 0.02-5.6% while preserving general capabilities. We further introduce attention-based interpretability metrics that diagnose failure modes at individual transformer layers for structured inputs, revealing how our approach reshapes internal attention patterns. Our results demonstrate that explicit execution semantics can be taught through standard post-training without architectural modification.

candidates.title: Development and Functional Demonstration of MedAnalysis Studio: A Locally Deployed Large Language Model Agent for Medical Research and Statistics Education
candidates.abstract: Objective: To develop a natural-language statistical-analysis agent that integrates a local large language model, specialized medical statistical tools, and output-checking stages, and to illustrate its functionality through representative software-interface displays.Materials and Methods: MedAnalysis Studio version 1.0.1 integrates a locally quantized Qwen2-family model, named EpiMind within the application, with structured tool calls, numerical traceability checks, and methodological auditing. The system provides Chinese and English interaction. Representative single-goal operations are illustrated by preserved screenshots of missingness reporting, correlation visualization, and event categorization.Results: The system comprises 93 configured tools in 12 modules. Illustrative software screenshots show a missingness-report panel, a correlation heatmap, and an event-status display within the natural-language workflow. These examples are presented as interface demonstrations rather than quantitative validation.Conclusions: The integrated workflow connects natural-language requests with explicit statistical operations, checking stages, and structured research outputs. Representative interface displays illustrate the organization of data-quality reporting, visualization, and outcome-category handling. Broader accuracy and clinical performance require separate evaluation.

candidates.title: Comparative evaluation of similarity metrics for Chinese retrieval augmented generation
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved impressive performance in natural language generation but remain vulnerable to hallucinations, particularly in Chinese short-text tasks where evidence grounding is essential. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) offers a promising solution, yet most prior studies rely on cosine similarity over a single embedding model and focus primarily on English benchmarks. In this study, we systematically evaluate eight similarity metrics—Jaccard, Weighted Jaccard, Dice, character n-gram Jaccard, Sentence-BERT cosine, Euclidean, Manhattan, and Levenshtein—together with two strong Chinese text embeddings (bge-base-zh-v1.5 and m3e-base) within a unified Chinese RAG pipeline. Using the complete CMRC2018 development set (3,219 questions), a second Chinese dataset (DuReader-robust, 1,417 questions), and two deterministically decoded generators (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), we report paired significance tests (McNemar exact; paired bootstrap) with Holm–Bonferroni correction and effect sizes. Four findings emerge. First, strong Chinese embeddings dominate retrieval on both datasets (bge: Recall@4 = 95.3% on CMRC2018, 98.3% on DuReader-robust), showing that the weak retrieval of the multilingual MiniLM SBERT encoder (62.5% on CMRC2018, 68.5% on DuReader-robust) is a property of that encoder rather than of embeddings per se. Second, once a length-bias implementation artifact is corrected, windowed character-level edit similarity attains Recall@4 = 93.8% and end-task F1/EM/grounding statistically indistinguishable from bge—without any embedding infrastructure. This advantage, however, is dataset-conditional: on DuReader-robust’s short keyword-style queries (mean 9.4 characters), which share few verbatim anchors with their source passages, the same lexical metrics fall to 55.8–67.6% and no longer beat even the multilingual SBERT baseline—bounding the scope of this finding to anchor-rich extractive QA. Third, resampling from full-set results shows that evaluations with n ≤ 100 select the wrong best method in up to 37.6% of draws, quantifying the risk of small-sample RAG studies. Fourth, method rankings are stable across the two generators at the tier level (Spearman ρ = 0.70–0.90) while absolute scores are strongly generator-dependent, and a single-threaded computational profile shows that competitive lexical retrieval needs no model weights at 17–22 ms per query, versus a 409 MB encoder and an 8–11 ms per-query encoding pass for the best embedding. For the datasets, encoders, and generators tested, these results provide statistically grounded, hardware-realistic guidance for building efficient and reliable Chinese RAG systems.

candidates.title: Large Language Models in Product Design: A Review
candidates.abstract: Product design is a complex, knowledge-based process that balances customer needs with engineering constraints and market realities. While traditional methods such as Quality Function Deployment (QFD) and machine learning (ML) have improved the design process and solutions, they still struggle with flexibility and a deep semantic understanding of design requirements. Advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), powered by Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), create new opportunities for intelligent, human-centred support for product design. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this systematic review analyzes 1,263 studies published between 2023 and 2026 to answer three questions: (1) how LLMs are applied across design stages, (2) how these systems are evaluated, and (3) what gaps remain. We found that LLMs successfully support design requirements analysis, ideation, and documentation. However, current evaluation methods lack standardized benchmarks for design quality. Persistent challenges remain, including hallucinations, weak domain grounding, tool-integration hurdles, and ethical concerns. To guide future research, we introduce a technical maturity map that highlights current achievements and uninvestigated areas in design systems and suggests a roadmap for applying LLMs in product design.

candidates.title: Correct-option surface profiles and composition sensitivity in industrial multimodal large language model evaluation
candidates.abstract: Industrial multimodal large language model (MLLM) benchmarks summarize performance with one accuracy, although that value also depends on test-set composition. We define a correct-option surface profile from relative word-like segment count, character length, question-option lexical overlap, and special expressions. Using 216,000 frozen responses to 2,400 MMAD-derived items, we audit specification robustness, adjusted associations, and profile-indexed consequences. Adjusted High-Low risk differences are 5.20-5.90 percentage points, but only 19 of 90 model-condition-context cells follow a strict Low-Medium-High order. Empirical composition profiles change standardized accuracy by -0.46 to +0.48 points relative to exact Balanced and produce four local point-order swaps in ten leaderboards, while Top-3 membership remains stable. The surface profile is therefore most informative for composition-aware interpretation of near-tied models, rather than as a stable shortcut-strength scale.

candidates.title: Keepace.ai: A Technical Report on a Large Language Model for Sports and Health
candidates.abstract: Large language models hold promise for delivering safe, scientifically grounded, and personalized exercise guidance at scale, yet the sports-and-health domain still lacks curated training corpora and rigorous evaluation benchmarks. Keepace (Keepace.ai) is a domain-specialized LLM built on Qwen3.5-27B through post-training, currently optimized for Chinese-language exercise guidance across three tasks: workout plan generation, sports-and-health knowledge QA, and personal sports data analysis. In internal rubric-based evaluations designed with domain experts, Keepace outperforms its base model and larger general-purpose baselines, with the most pronounced improvements in exercise safety, boundary compliance, structured output completeness, and scientific accuracy. This report summarizes the current design, data pipeline, safety-first evaluation framework, and evaluation results of Keepace.

candidates.title: Time-Decay-Aware Reasoning: Maintaining Large Language Model Knowledge Freshness Without Full Retraining
candidates.abstract: Large language models store factual knowledge in their parameters, but this knowledge is fixed at the training cut-off point and becomes outdated as the world changes; therefore, although fluent, the answers may be incorrect. A time-decay-aware reasoning framework has been introduced in this paper to maintain such knowledge over time without retraining or modifying the model’s parameters. The framework assigns a decay rate to each fact based on how often it is updated in a temporal knowledge base, converts this rate into the probability that a parametric answer has expired, and only issues a retrieval call when this probability exceeds a threshold; thus, retrieval is focused on facts that have actually aged. On TempLAMA (50,310 temporally scoped Wikidata questions, 2010–2020), the method outperforms the fine-tuning and editing baselines, recovers about two-thirds of the accuracy gap between a frozen model and exhaustive retrieval while issuing only half as many retrieval calls; it does not modify static knowledge. The Design aims to run large language models efficiently in the face of continuous fact updates.

candidates.title: Text-to-SQL in the Era of Large Language Models: A Survey of Reasoning-Centric and Efficiency-Centric Approaches
candidates.abstract: Text-to-SQL translates natural-language questions into executable SQL, enabling non-expert access to relational databases. Despite advances in large language models (LLMs), reliable systems must ground questions in schemas and values, handle large schemas, and preserve semantic correctness. This survey reviews the evolution toward LLM-based and agentic systems through an objective-oriented taxonomy of Reasoning-Centric (RC) and Efficiency-Centric (EC) approaches. RC emphasizes interpretation, grounding, workflow organization, candidate search, and verification; EC emphasizes acquiring, adapting, transferring, and deploying capabilities under identifiable resource or deployment constraints. Assignments reflect a study’s stated objectives and main contribution, not model size, openness, or training strategy alone. We connect three recurring challenges to ten methodological families and provide an evidence-linked inventory of 114 studies with eleven boundary interpretations. Benchmark-aware comparisons retain model, split, metric, and inference-budget distinctions, including twelve illustrative BIRD development configurations from ten studies. Explicit token values are reported by 31 of 114 studies; a further 6 additional approximate, range, or bound disclosures bring the total to 37, including 16 of the 50 representative studies. Heterogeneous scopes, spanning prompt context, pipeline components, dataset totals, and offline generation, limit direct comparison of end-to-end inference consumption. These findings motivate configuration-specific resource reporting. We also discuss security and safety risks and their evaluation implications. The taxonomy, comparisons, and reporting framework support joint analysis of reasoning quality and resource use in systems combining RC and EC mechanisms.

candidates.title: Systematic Framework of Application Methods for Large Language Models in Language Sciences
candidates.abstract: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming language sciences. However, their widespread deployment currently suffers from methodological fragmentation and a lack of systematic soundness. This study proposes two comprehensive methodological frame works designed to guide the strategic and responsible application of LLMs inlanguage sciences. The first method-selection framework defines and systematizes three distinct, complementary approaches, each linked toa specific research goal: (1) prompt-based interaction with general-usemodels for exploratory analysis and hypothesis generation; (2) fine tuning of open-source models for confirmatory, theory-driven investigation and high-quality data generation; and (3) extraction of contextualized embeddings for further quantitative analysis and probing of model internal mechanisms. We detail the technical implementationand inherent trade-offs of each method, supported by empirical casestudies. Based on the method-selection framework, the second systematic framework proposed provides constructed configurations that guide the practical implementation of multi-stage research pipelines based on these approaches. We then conducted a series of empirical experiments to validate our proposed framework, employing retrospective analysis, prospective application, and an expert evaluation survey. By enforcing the strategic alignment of research questions with the appropriate LLM methodology, the frameworks enable a critical paradigm shift in language science research. We believe that this systemis fundamental for ensuring reproducibility, facilitating the criticalevaluation of LLM mechanisms, and providing the structure necessaryto move traditional linguistics from ad-hoc utility to verifiable, robust science.

candidates.title: Research on Evaluation of Large Language Models for Healthcare
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) constitute a new growth engine for artificial intelligence, boasting tremendous potential to reshape the healthcare industry. When deploying LLMs to empower healthcare scenarios, scientific and comprehensive evaluation is an indispensable task, which can effectively mitigate potential risks and guarantee service quality. This paper elaborates on the evaluation contents and methodologies for LLMs oriented toward healthcare, and identifies key research priorities for future exploration. The work provides references for academic research and industrial practice concerning the evaluation of medical LLMs, enabling LLMs to exert greater positive impacts across the healthcare sector.

candidates.title: Large Language Models (LLMs) for Research Knowledge Discovery
candidates.abstract: The growth of the scholarly literature has posed numerous challenges to knowledge discovery and synthesis and research efficiency. Large Language Models (LLMs), founded on the transformer architecture and other state-of-the-art tools like BERT and GPT-type models, have a tremendous potential to revolutionize the way researchers conduct their scholarly work. This chapter evaluates the role that LLMs play in shaping research practices through literature search, evidence screening, knowledge synthesis, hypothesis generation, and academic writing. The chapter offers an evidence-based review of LLMs in the different stages of the research process with the use of the summary tables on model development, application areas, challenges, and examples from various disciplines. Additionally, critical limitations of the current tools will be discussed alongside suggestions for future directions.

candidates.title: Large Language Model-Assisted Multimodal Federated Sensing for Compliance Risk Screening in Cross-Border Trade
candidates.abstract: With the continuous expansion of cross-border agricultural supply chains, reliable food-safety risk screening under decentralized data ownership, heterogeneous sensing equipment, and jurisdiction-dependent, non-stationary regulatory limits pose a fundamental challenge to intelligent inspection systems. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an LLM-assisted regulation-aware heterogeneous multimodal federated learning framework that establishes a three-tier decoupling architecture. First, an available-modality and quality-adaptive fusion mechanism dynamically weights RGB images, near-infrared (NIR) spectra, and environmental time-series while enforcing strict zero weighting on unavailable modalities and continuous suppression of degraded observations. Second, a regulation-independent state-prototype collaboration and personalized federated learning strategy is developed on a unified continuous concentration scale, enabling cross-institutional transfer of physical contamination representations while avoiding the use of jurisdiction-dependent compliance labels to define shared prototype groups and preserving client-specific adapters against non-IID drift. Third, offline large language model (LLM) parsing transforms unstructured multi-jurisdictional trade regulations into machine-executable rule bases, which are coupled with an uncertainty-aware risk calibration module to dynamically determine exceedance probabilities and reinspection recommendations without retraining front-end sensing encoders when regulatory standards shift. Experimental evaluations on a multisource maize and aflatoxin B1 screening dataset in a workstation-based federated simulation demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.054±0.002 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.078±0.003, while elevating the area under the curve (AUC) and F1-score to 0.862±0.008 and 0.833±0.009, respectively, reducing the false negative rate (FNR) to 0.121±0.007 (p<0.001). Under severe client heterogeneity and missing-modality scenarios, the proposed approach maintains an AUC of 0.823±0.010 and an F1-score of 0.796±0.011. Ablation and ownership-level analyses assess robustness, calibration (expected calibration error of 0.032), and regulatory adaptation with fixed sensing encoders, providing an end-to-end, traceable decision-support paradigm for international agricultural trade screening.

candidates.title: Jailbreak Connectivity: Towards Diverse, Transferable, and Universal Multimodal Large Language Model Jailbreak
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are vulnerable to visual jailbreak attacks that bypass safety safeguards. Existing methods typically optimize isolated adversarial examples, limiting attack diversity, transferability, and generalization. We propose Jailbreak Connectivity (JC), a framework based on the observation that effective adversarial inputs can be connected through low-loss regions in image space. JC optimizes continuous adversarial paths: path sampling yields diverse jailbreak images, lightweight surrogate classifiers guide cross-model transfer, and a distribution-level objective enables universal attacks across harmful queries. On MM-SafetyBench, JC achieves average attack success rates of 84.01%, 85.77%, and 97.95% on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B-IT, respectively, exceeding the strongest baselines by up to 68.36 percentage points. In black-box evaluations, JC improves attack success rates over FigStep by 24.69 and 27.34 percentage points on GPT-5.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, respectively. These findings reveal structured vulnerabilities in MLLM safety alignment and inform more comprehensive security evaluation.

candidates.title: Human-in-the-loop annotation and review platform for dental panoramic radiographs: a comparative evaluation of multimodal large language models in tooth-level abnormality detection
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly explored for medical image interpretation, yet their capability for tooth-level abnormality detection on dental panoramic radiographs (OPG) remains largely unquantified. Moreover, reference-standard construction for such evaluations usually lacks a transparent human-in-the-loop review pipeline. We developed an interactive web-based review platform with multi-view visualization (original and annotated images), finding-by-finding auditing, and FDI tooth-number recommendation with accept/reject/manual confirmation, from which an expert-reviewed OPG reference standard of 233 cases, admitted by consensus verification of two senior oral clinicians (1,859 tooth–finding pairs across 1,600 annotated tooth positions; FDI tooth numbers and a closed 20-class disease vocabulary), was derived. On this reference standard, we compared four MLLMs — doubao_web, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, Gemini-3.6-flash-medium and M365 Copilot (GPT 5.6) — on two tasks: tooth-level finding presence and tooth–finding association (classification). The four models were accessed through two arms, an API arm and a consumer web arm, which were not run under matched conditions; within-arm contrasts are the primary inference and cross-arm contrasts are descriptive. Precision, recall and F1 were computed with case-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals; paired binary outcomes were tested with exact McNemar tests, re-estimated under case-level cluster-robust variance with Holm correction; per-case F1 with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests; and inter-model error independence with Cohen’s kappa. The 233-case evaluation set was drawn from a corpus compiled from an openly licensed public collection together with radiographs acquired at the Department of Stomatology, Yijishan Hospital of Wannan Medical College, with all patient-identifiable information removed before analysis; the study was approved by the institutional ethics committee. M365 Copilot GPT 5.6 showed the highest point estimates on both tasks (tooth F1 = 0.642, pair F1 = 0.485), followed by Gemini-3.6-flash-medium (0.610/0.456). Within the web arm, M365 significantly outperformed doubao_web (0.501/0.348; both \(p < 0.001\) ); within the API arm, Gemini significantly outperformed Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct (0.537/0.340; both \(p < 0.001\) ). The cross-arm gap between M365 and Gemini was borderline in per-case tooth F1 ( p = 0.052) and remained significant in the tooth-level McNemar test under case-level cluster-robust variance ( p = 0.005; Holm-adjusted p = 0.010). The two strongest models were positively correlated ( \(\kappa\) = 0.316), while all other pairwise model \(\kappa\) values were negative ( \(-0.203\) to \(-0.007\) ), indicating largely independent error patterns. All models performed poorly on caries and periapical lesions (pair F1 < 0.1). Current MLLMs performed relatively better on high-contrast structures (e.g., impacted teeth, F1 = 0.831 for M365, 0.814 for Gemini-3.6) but remained inadequate for subtle lesions; the errors of the four models were largely independent rather than complementary, and a two-model cross-check improved tooth-level union recall from 0.668 to 0.727–0.854 at the cost of arbitrating 20.4–42.3% of positive teeth (a descriptive cross-model quantification, given the unmatched access arms), which supports a two-model cross-check plus human review workflow when that arbitration cost is acceptable. The proposed review platform provides a reproducible, audit-trail reference-standard construction pipeline for benchmarking MLLMs in dental imaging.

candidates.title: Grid-Coded Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Hybrid Retrieval for Minute-Level Aircraft Trajectory Prediction
candidates.abstract: Ultra-short-term (1–5 min) tactical trajectory prediction underpins air traffic conflict detection, yet deep learning models such as long short-term memory (LSTM), gated recurrent unit (GRU) and multilayer perceptron (MLP) networks lack an aviation spatial inductive bias, fit sparse grid-transition samples poorly, and in the small-sample setting studied here incur position errors an order of magnitude larger than trivial baselines. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a natural remedy, replacing parametric fitting with non-parametric retrieval of historical flight priors and requiring no retraining. Existing RAG schemes nevertheless break down on gridded airspace: character-hash encoding of grid identifiers discards spatial semantics, so adjacent grids are treated as unrelated, and the transition prior of the current grid is often missed, while stochastic vector search offers no recall guarantee, so such a miss silently collapses the prediction to persistence. This paper therefore proposes RAG-Hybrid, a grid-coded dual-path framework in which a deterministic breadth-first search (BFS) lookup reconstructs the local transition subgraph of the current grid from the knowledge base, spatially aware FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) retrieval draws on a training-free focal-weighted Gaussian grid vectorisation, and Laplace smoothing with global-Markov weighting calibrates the resulting transition matrix. The evaluation uses Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast (ADS-B) trajectories from 62 test flights over a 0.25° × 0.25° grid covering Central–South China, and reports 1 min to 5 min horizons. On this test set, the framework holds single-step Top-1 at 0.7097, identical to a leakage-free global-Markov baseline and within one standard error of the trivial persistence predictor (0.7581), while raising Top-3 and Top-5 at the +1 min horizon from 0.9355 to 0.9839. A constant-velocity dead-reckoning baseline attains the highest point accuracy at this horizon (Top-1 0.8065, MAE 4.90 km) but returns a single cell, so the framework exceeds it on Top-5 by 0.1774. The one component effect that this study resolves statistically is the deterministic lookup channel at the far end of the horizon: removing it cuts the pooled five-step Top-5 hit rate from 0.7452 to 0.6516 and the +5 min Top-5 hit rate from 0.5645 to 0.3710.

candidates.title: Fu-TCM: a multimodal large language model that learns traditional Chinese medicine diagnostic reasoning
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are advancing in multimodal understanding and reasoning, accelerating medical model development. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) uses evidence from the four examinations to determine disease location and nature, differentiate syndromes and guide treatment. This diagnostic process constitutes a complete chain of reasoning. We present Fu-TCM, a multimodal TCM LLM trained on data retained after cleaning and filtering an initial collection of approximately 7.12 million examples derived from classical texts, textbooks, medical images, clinical cases and publicly available datasets. The model was further optimized using Bianzheng-Grounded Policy Optimization (BGPO), which explicitly targets syndrome differentiation through rewards for response format, intermediate TCM reasoning fields and final syndrome predictions. Fu-TCM-27B led all six benchmarks spanning TCM reasoning, text and vision, achieving a macro-average accuracy of 81.01% and surpassing the strongest reference model with complete results across all six benchmarks by 7.13 percentage points. Its largest margin was 11.90 points on Fu-bianzheng. Case-level analyses further showed a positive association between intermediate-field accuracy and final syndrome-selection accuracy in most evaluated models. These findings suggest that TCM syndrome differentiation may be computationally learnable and that structured reasoning supervision can improve performance across TCM tasks.

candidates.title: Does Chain-of-Thought Reliance Follow a Scaling Law?Larger Models Follow Their Steps More, Independent of Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Monitoring a model's chain of thought (CoT) is useful for safety only if the final answer depends on the written steps. Prior measurements use natural tasks where true reasoning is unknown. We measure it against an exact ground truth on a synthetic box-swap task where every intermediate state is known. We replace one step inside a model's own chain with a wrong but valid state and check whether the answer follows the edit. We evaluate 25 open-weight models--Qwen3 (0.6B-14B, base and post-trained), Gemma 3 (1B-12B), Llama 3 (1B-8B), and 8 OLMo 2 checkpoints--on 7,200 items each. We find five results: (1) Reliance rises with size and saturates. In Qwen3, answer reliance rises from 16-18% at 0.6B to 97-100% at 14B; a logistic in log N fits well (R^2 = 0.89), and Gemma 3 and Llama 3 follow this trend. (2) Capability is the main driver. Across all models, reliance and step accuracy correlate at r = 0.99; equally capable models are equally reliant, regardless of family. (3) Size still matters at matched correctness. On problems solved correctly before the edit, reliance increases with size among capable models (rho = 0.80, p = 0.002). (4) Post-training does not change reliance. Base and post-trained Qwen3 differ by at most 0.03 from 4B upward; a large gap at 1.7B matches a large capability gap. (5) No model up to 14B solves the task internally. Without written steps, every capable model is at chance once a problem has four or more swaps. OLMo 2 checkpoints never become capable, making the training-token axis a limitation. On tasks requiring step-by-step computation, scale makes the chain of thought more load-bearing, supporting CoT monitoring in this regime.

candidates.title: Can large language models complement tourism surveys?
candidates.abstract: Tourism research relies heavily on surveys, yet declining response rates challenge data collection. Large language models offer a potential alternative for approximating human responses. This study compares four prompting techniques using ChatGPT-4o. At the mean level, chain-of-thought and role-based prompting showed limited alignment with human data, while bias mitigation yielded slight improvement. N-shot learning achieved the strongest mean-level alignment, although performance varied across measures. Analyses of variance, skewness, and kurtosis showed that no prompting technique consistently reproduced human response distributions. These findings identify important boundary conditions: large language models may approximate the “average respondent” on specific measures but fail to capture broader distributional properties, supporting their potential use for early-stage pretesting and screening rather than inference-driven research.

candidates.title: An Automatic Evaluation Model for Health Science Popularization Short Videos Generated by Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Using multimodal large language model (LLMs) to generate and popularize short health-science videos can significantly shorten their production cycle. This practice plays a vital role in lowering the public’s access threshold to health knowledge and promoting the high-quality dissemination of scientific health popularization content. However, due to the limitations of creators, regulators and multimodal LLMs themselves, these generated short videos may still lead to the spread of misleading health knowledge, posing potential risks to public health cognition. Therefore, it is urgent to construct a systematic and automatic evaluation system for such health science popularization short videos. In this paper, we propose an automatic evaluation model for such short videos by leveraging the well-known Source-Channel-Recipient (SCR) framework in the field of information communication. This automatic evaluation model includes three parts: an automatic review mechanism for Source, an automatic technology-optimization mechanism for Channel, and an automatic feedback-optimization mechanism for Recipient.

candidates.title: A SHAP-Guided Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework for Predictive Maintenance Decision Support
candidates.abstract: Abstract Predictive maintenance models can reach high detection performance, but their outputs often remain difficult to operationalize in industrial environments, where maintenance decisions require interpretability and actionable guidance. Existing approaches rarely establish a direct link between failure predictions, model explanations, and maintenance-oriented recommendations. This study proposes a proof-of-concept framework that extends retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to tabular predictive maintenance data through SHAP-guided query construction. A supervised machine learning model is trained to predict machine failures from operational data. SHAP explanations are then extracted to identify the dominant factors driving each prediction and converted into structured queries. These queries guide retrieval from an experimental maintenance knowledge base using embedding-based similarity search. The retrieved information is used by a generation module to produce case-specific maintenance recommendations aligned with the predictive output and its explanation. The framework is evaluated on a benchmark predictive maintenance dataset, where the predictive model shows strong failure detection capability, with particular improvement in recall for rare failure events. The retrieval module further indicates that explanation-derived queries can retrieve semantically relevant maintenance information. The results support the feasibility of integrating predictive modeling, SHAP-based explanation, retrieval, and LLM-based generation for maintenance-oriented interpretation. The proposed framework remains a proof of concept and does not yet constitute a fully validated industrial decision-support system.

candidates.title: GAAC: Lossless KV Compression for Bandwidth-Efficient LLM Inference on Personal Devices
candidates.abstract: Weight-only, lossy quantization substantially reduces the storage and memory requirements for serving large language models (LLMs), but the growing key-value (KV) cache remains a bottleneck for long-context inference on personal devices. We present Group-Adaptive Additive Codec (GAAC), a lossless KV compression and serving system that exploits exponent redundancy to reduce storage and accelerate attention without introducing KV approximation. GAAC encodes BF16 exponents using calibrated per-channel base-plus-offset codes over contiguous ranges. GAAC adapts code widths across small groups while preserving KV values bit-for-bit. A fused attention kernel reconstructs KV tiles on the fly, avoiding full-cache decompression. Block-wise compression and fixed-capacity slots support incremental cache updates and paged serving. Across five tested models, GAAC achieves 1.405-1.407$\times$ lossless BF16 KV compression. We also study compression performance on low-precision tensors FP8 E4M3 caches ( 1.09-1.14$\times$) and E5M2 caches (1.25-1.30$\times$). On NVIDIA DGX Spark, GAAC accelerates decode attention at a 64K-token context by 1.19-1.27$\times$ and end-to-end W4A16 decode steps by 1.04-1.15$\times$. In serving, it reduces resident KV memory by approximately 26% and increases aggregate throughput by 13-29% under comparable KV-memory budgets. On Apple M4, GAAC achieves 1.02-1.25$\times$ attention speedups, demonstrating portability beyond NVIDIA GPUs.

candidates.title: Machine psychology for language models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show increasingly advanced emergent capabilities and are being incorporated across various societal domains. Understanding their behavior and reasoning abilities is therefore important. We argue that a fruitful direction for research is engaging LLMs in experiments inspired by psychology that have traditionally been aimed at understanding human cognition and behavior. Here, we highlight and summarize theoretical perspectives, experimental paradigms, and computational analysis techniques that this approach brings to the table. It paves the way for a "machine psychology" for LLMs that goes beyond performance measurements and focuses instead on computational insights that move us toward a better understanding and discovery of emergent abilities and behavioral patterns in LLMs. We review existing work taking this approach, synthesize best practices, and highlight promising future directions. We also describe the important caveats of applying methodologies designed for understanding humans to machines. We posit that leveraging tools from experimental psychology to study LLMs will become increasingly valuable as models evolve to be more powerful, opaque, multimodal, and integrated into complex agentic real-world settings.

candidates.title: When Visual Evidence Is Insufficient: How Instructions, Post-Training, and Internal Activations Shape Refusal in Multimodal Language Models
candidates.abstract: For reliable deployment, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) should recognize when an image provides insufficient evidence to answer a question and withhold unsupported answers. Yet refusal alone is not necessarily evidence of such recognition: models may refuse because of unrelated safety constraints or without identifying the missing evidence. We study how refusal on visually unanswerable questions is shaped by three sources of control: inference-time instructions, post-training, and internal activation interventions. Across three MLLMs on the MoHoBench benchmark, we systematically manipulate the meaning and placement of refusal instructions, compare supervised and preference-based post-training, and intervene on a refusal-related activation direction derived from naturally answered and refused examples. We find that refusal is highly sensitive to both the meaning and placement of instructions, with model-specific changes at the sample level that are obscured by aggregate refusal rates. Evidence-aware and general refusal instructions have stronger effects than an intentionally mismatched safety instruction. Post-training produces larger increases in refusal, but can also induce responses that combine refusal language with attempted answers. In contrast, activation intervention produces smaller yet transferable changes across prompt conditions, without evidence of indiscriminate refusal on tested visually answerable samples. These findings show that refusal is jointly shaped by external instructions, post-training, and internal representations, highlighting the need to disentangle evidence recognition from a model's learned propensity to refuse.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for Reliable AI Question Answering
candidates.abstract: This paper presents a review of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for reliable AI question answering. Large Language Models (LLMs) can sometimes generate incorrect, unsupported, or outdated information. RAG addresses these limitations by retrieving relevant information from external knowledge sources and using it to generate context-aware answers. This paper explains the fundamental architecture and working principles of RAG, including document preprocessing, embedding generation, vector-based retrieval, context construction, and answer generation. It also discusses the proposed RAG framework and evaluation metrics such as answer accuracy, faithfulness, context precision, context recall, and response latency. Furthermore, the paper examines practical applications of RAG in education, healthcare information, customer support, enterprise knowledge management, and research assistance. It discusses key challenges, including retrieval errors, hallucinations, data quality, security, and computational cost. Finally, it highlights future research directions for improving retrieval quality, evidence grounding, and reliable AI question answering. The paper concludes that RAG can support more context-aware and evidence-based answers, but its reliability depends on source quality, retrieval effectiveness, context selection, and answer verification.
