candidates.title: Reranking Answers of Large Language Models with Knowledge Graphs
candidates.abstract: Answering natural language questions over knowledge graph data is challenging due to the vast number of facts, which can be difficult to process and navigate. One potential solution for this issue is to use mined subgraphs related to the query, although this process still requires extracting these subgraphs. This research presents a solution for extracting subgraphs related to entity candidates from a question-and-answer set, which can be obtained by inferring a large language model by calculating the shortest paths between entities. The proposed approaches detail various features that can be extracted from the subgraphs and reranking models to select the most probable answers from a list of candidates. Experiments were conducted on Wikidata to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed approaches. This involved enumerating all the main feature types that can be extracted from mined subgraphs and a detailed analysis of the proposed features and reranking method combinations. In addition, a public web application that provides a useful web tool for studying the graph space between question and answer entities has been developed to work with subgraphs. This includes visualization of the extracted subgraph and automatic generation of natural language text to describe it.

candidates.title: Quality-Controlled Reply and Summary Data for Post-Training Small Language Models in AI Call-Screening Agents
candidates.abstract: Small language models have improved to the point where a phone can plausibly screen its own calls, answering on an absent owner's behalf without sending call content off the device, a privacy-respecting alternative to cloud call handling. Realizing that promise takes a model that can do two things well: reply within the owner's authority during the call, and afterward tell the owner what happened and what needs attention. Released small models do neither reliably - they raise unwarranted alarms about ordinary callers and write summaries that drop material conditions or report a caller's claims as fact - and real calls supply no reference replies or summaries to learn from. We construct supervision for both tasks from synthetic calls under an information-boundary constraint: a caller writer works from a private scenario brief, a reply writer sees only the conversation up to the current turn, and a summary writer sees the completed transcript. Separate model-based reviews of the full dialogue and the summary decide which calls enter training, yielding a corpus of 3,395 calls with 15,102 targets (11,707 reply, 3,395 summary). Training a single shared LoRA adapter on both tasks, we evaluate six models (0.6-4B parameters) before and after adaptation on 192 held-out calls. Reply qualification rises from 21-54% to 94-97% and summary qualification from 0-6% to 43-72%; all twelve paired gains (six models x two tasks) have bootstrap intervals above zero, and the summary gains hold in every source family. Because one model both screened the training data and scored the outputs, these rates measure agreement with that evaluator's standard rather than human acceptance, which a planned human study will test. After adaptation, coherence and naturalness failures nearly vanish, leaving grounding and usefulness - faithfully tracking who said what, under which conditions - as the remaining challenge.

candidates.title: Large Language Models in Hearing Care
candidates.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) may support hearing care, but evidence of clinical benefit remains unclear. We conducted a scoping review across eight databases, with searches updated in September 2026. Among 110 included reports, 95 empirical analysis units comprised 62 model-centered benchmarks, 31 application-oriented investigations, and two adoption surveys. Applications addressed assessment scoring, clinical documentation, rehabilitation content, biomedical evidence processing, psychosocial support, and research. Fourteen empirical units evaluated prototypes or target users; none tested prospective service deployment or comparative clinical impact. Privacy evaluation concerned attitudes or perceived confidentiality; no included study tested technical privacy safeguards. Current evidence supports selected task-specific capabilities, not established improvements in care. Future research should prioritize applications addressing defined hearing-care needs and compare them with usual care or simpler alternatives. Evaluation should measure patient and professional benefit, safety, privacy, accessibility, and workload rather than response accuracy alone.

candidates.title: Experimental reasoning in large language models
candidates.abstract: Scientific reasoning requires interaction with the physical world: designing experiments, interpreting outcomes, and deciding what experiment should come next. Here we show that general-purpose large language models (LLMs) already possess substantial capabilities for experimental reasoning. We connected LLMs to a liquid-handling robot and camera through PEARL, which provides perception, action, and persistent state. Given objectives rather than prescribed workflows, the system designed and successfully executed experiments, interpreted observations, and revised its approach as evidence accumulated. When information was insufficient, PEARL autonomously designed and performed intermediate experiments to acquire it. In quantitative enzyme characterization, it judged whether measurements were sufficient, new data were required, or conditions needed to change. Across eight scenarios, these behaviors were reliable with limited agent scaffolding and no supplied scenario-specific recovery recipes.More broadly, general-purpose LLMs may provide a reasoning layer between scientific objectives and physical experimentation, shifting laboratory automation from executing predefined procedures toward AI systems that participate directly in the experimental process.

candidates.title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
candidates.abstract: A synopsis in novels folds a story into a few lines; a function in code gathers many steps with a single execution. Context editing is native to language itself. In this paper, we propose the Native Context Editing (NCE) framework, which gives language model agents a grammar for natively editing their own context. By encoding context-editing operations in a grammar of dedicated special tokens, we teach the agents to invoke edits through the language itself. We train agents on iteratively constructed trajectory segments, with each teacher edit conditioned on the evolving context. This establishes context editing as an atomic and inherent capability of LLM agents, enabling them to dynamically modify their context as they generate responses over long-horizon reasoning and interaction. Compared with context-editing methods that learn to generate tool-use code within specific external harness environments, our approach integrates context editing as an internal mechanism of the model's native generation process, enabling better generalization across diverse real-world workflows. On four long-horizon agentic benchmarks (Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, and SWE-bench Pro), NCE improves the average task success rate over the base model by 5.6 percentage points for LongCat-Flash-Lite-Sparse and by 4.5 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, while reducing average token usage by 36% and 15%, respectively.

candidates.title: Structure over Reasoning: Unified Zero-Shot Navigation with a Small Vision-Language Model
candidates.abstract: Vision-language navigation is moving into photorealistic, physically simulated scenes, where the leading zero-shot agents put a vision-language model in the control loop to choose every move and stop. Robots favour small models, whose abilities are uneven: Qwen3-VL-4B can judge whether a single view looks like the goal, but its route reasoning is at chance, its distance estimates nearly constant, its stop votes unreliable. Our agent therefore asks it two perceptual questions per step, which direction looks like the goal and whether the view justifies stopping, plus one gated frontier query on route-bearing instructions, and treats the answers as evidence, not actions: a route-blind semantic field over a bird's-eye map accumulates the directional scores through a tempered update, a skeleton graph supplies frontiers and geodesic distances, and a two-stage terminator turns stop votes into termini through a trail-consistency gate and a budget-forced return. With every baseline re-run in one installation at one budget, the agent exceeds all four zero-shot baselines of the VLNVerse subset in mean success on both granularities, though the paired interval against the strongest coarse-grained baseline includes zero. Termination is the dominant lever in ablation, thirteen attempts to give the model more of the navigation establish no reliable gain, and the agent runs on a Unitree Go2 quadruped with off-board inference. Code, per-episode logs and a robot video will be released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/structure-over-reasoning-PAGE.

candidates.title: Benchmark for Structured Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Perovskite Photovoltaics
candidates.abstract: While retrieval-augmented language models increasingly serve as literature assistants in the physical sciences, existing benchmarks evaluate them primarily on qualitative text overlap or through model-based scoring rather than against verified experimental ground truth. In experimental materials disciplines such as perovskite photovoltaics, however, the most critical inquiries are inherently quantitative and aggregate measurements across dozens or hundreds of papers. Here, we present a quantitative question-answering benchmark where all 755 ground-truth answers are computed directly from 45,441 measured device records (40,889 human-curated records through 2021 and 4,552 records extracted from 2022-2026 literature). Benchmarking six retrieval architectures over 158,274 passages from 25,662 papers using an open 14B model on a single 24 GB GPU, standard passage retrieval tops out at 16-23% accuracy (compared to 1.6-6.5% zero-shot). In contrast, equipping the language model with read-only SQL execution over the structured device table elevates accuracy to 51.5% on historical and 50.8% on prospective literature -- a 33.01.8 percentage-point advantage over hybrid text retrieval. Aggregate queries spanning extrema, distributions, and filtered record counts prove virtually unsolvable via text retrieval alone, demonstrating that systematic table extraction is an operational prerequisite for literature-scale quantitative inquiry.

candidates.title: Conformal Prediction-Enabled Sequence-level Policy Optimization for Reasoning Language Models
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning improves the reasoning capability of large language models through verifiable rewards for mathematical and coding tasks. In token-level methods such as GRPO, clipping acts on individual token ratios while the reward and advantage apply to a complete response. Recent sequence-level methods align these units but still use fixed clipping bands, whose tail probabilities change as the score distribution evolves. We propose Conformal Prediction-Enabled Sequence-level Policy Optimization (CSPO), which adaptively calibrates sequence-level clipping bounds using recent training statistics. The resulting band targets a specified marginal tail budget and adapts to policy drift; calibration conditional on response length requires additional assumptions. We bound the probability that a fresh score falls outside the band by the target miscoverage level plus explicit CDF discrepancy and drift terms. Under additional moment conditions, this bound also controls the objective and gradient error relative to the unclipped GSPO power surrogate. Experiments with the Qwen3-1.7B series show improvements over GSPO on difficult mathematical reasoning benchmarks and ALFWorld, with clipping endpoints that adapt during training.

candidates.title: Bud ContextCompact 2.0: Context Compaction for Agent Success and Accuracy with Small Language Models and Constrained Context Windows
candidates.abstract: Agents that work for many turns outgrow the context window of the model that serves them, and on small language models (SLMs) and constrained inference systems that window is small. Context compaction replaces older turns with a summary so a session can continue, but it is lossy, costs a model call, and can help or hurt depending on when it runs. We describe Bud ContextCompact 2.0, the compaction built into the Bud agent runtime, and evaluate it in two settings. On recall questions over recorded agent sessions, compaction to a 16K budget raised a 1.2B-parameter model's accuracy to 0.335, from 0.247 with truncation and 0.176 with its full 32K history (p < 0.001), and raised a 9B model from 0.515 (truncation) to 0.577 (p = 0.04). On 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks run end to end by a 27B reasoning model on a 49K-token window (556 graded sessions), compaction raised the resolve rate on long sessions from 41% to 53% (+12.3 points, 95% CI +1.6 to +23.0, McNemar p = 0.043), left short sessions unchanged, and used 13% fewer tokens per solved task at equal total cost. The main failure without compaction was not the history overflowing but a reasoning turn exhausting the room the history left. The gain has limits: it vanished under a 45-minute session budget, because each summary took a median of 161 s, and in a threshold study it appeared only when compaction triggered early enough to leave room. An 8B model submitted after about ten turns at 5-8K tokens and never needed compaction. We argue that the accuracy results transfer across hardware, including CPU inference, for an equivalent model and window, while the time cost scales with the hardware and must be budgeted for.

candidates.title: ATEST: Adaptive Resource-Aware Test-Time Scaling for LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling multiple answers, but fixed sampling budgets ignore both query difficulty and the changing energy cost of inference under GPU contention. We measure up to a 4.1-fold increase in energy for the same four-sample query as GPU load rises. We present ATEST, a resource-aware TTS framework that jointly considers the expected value of additional samples and their current GPU cost. ATEST-Online, its default mode, requires no offline calibration: it incrementally generates samples, estimates the stability of the plurality answer, monitors live GPU conditions, and learns step energy cost online to decide when to stop. ATEST-Calibrated instead selects a per-query budget using offline accuracy and cost models, favoring deployments with stable loads. We evaluate both modes on four reasoning and question-answering datasets using Phi-3-mini on an NVIDIA A100 under controlled varying load, and test transfer to an NVIDIA L40S and Qwen2.5-3B. Across the four A100 datasets, ATEST-Online answers every query without exceeding the energy budget, while achieving the highest or statistically tied accuracy and reducing sampling as load increases. On GSM8K at high load, it achieves 60.0% accuracy with no deferrals, versus 44.0% accuracy and 42.4% deferrals for ATEST-Calibrated. Ablations show that online cost learning drives adaptation to load. Including offline profiling, ATEST-Online uses 42 times less GPU time and 48 times less energy than ATEST-Calibrated for the evaluated workload. Online control trades higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks for robustness under varying load; offline calibration remains competitive under stable conditions.

candidates.title: Large Language Model Agents for Autonomous Scientific Research: A Lifecycle Survey of Methods, Systems, Benchmarks, and Risks
candidates.abstract: Large language models have moved from passive text generators to autonomous agents that plan, use tools, and act across the scientific research process. A fast-growing body of work now targets every stage of that process, from literature search and hypothesis generation through experiment code, wet-lab automation, manuscript writing, and peer review, together with discipline-specific agents for chemistry, biology, materials, medicine, and mathematics and a large family of benchmarks built to measure them. This review combines a systematic search with a narrative synthesis. A protocol-driven search of arXiv, Semantic Scholar, bioRxiv, and fourteen conference proceedings, run to 30 May 2026, retrieved 2928 records, of which 883 met the eligibility criteria and were coded, and 253 were analysed in depth. We organize that literature along the scientific research lifecycle and cross-cut it by four design axes, namely agent architecture, learning mechanism, autonomy level, and validation regime, and we report the publication status and evidence level of every claim we rely on. The field has matured unevenly. Retrieval-grounded deep research and machine learning engineering show repeatable gains on peer-reviewed benchmarks, whereas open-ended ideation, end-to-end discovery, and trustworthy reporting remain fragile. Realistic benchmarks report success rates between one sixth and one third, with a Kaggle bronze medal on 16.9 percent of engineering competitions, a best replication score of 21.0 percent across 20 published papers, 32.4 percent of scientific coding tasks solved, and 31.5 percent accuracy on memorization-resistant equation discovery. On a three-paper subset of the replication benchmark, an o1 agent scores 26.6 percent against 41.4 percent for machine learning PhDs. Closed-loop discovery systems report results confirmed in the wet lab, and all three such systems in our master comparison remain preprints, which places those claims on weaker evidential footing than the benchmark results. A reliability gap runs through the whole lifecycle, as agents that retrieve and write fluently still fabricate results, miscite sources, and overstate confidence. We contribute a documented search and coding protocol with the full coded corpus made available, a unified taxonomy, a master comparison of systems, a structured account of benchmarks and metrics, and a risk-to-mitigation map, and we close with a maturity assessment and a research roadmap for safe and verifiable autonomous science.

candidates.title: HALLUCINATION IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS: CAUSES, DETECTION, AND MITIGATION STRATEGIES
candidates.abstract: One of the common problems with LLMs (Large Language Models) is that they sometimes produce fluent text that deviates from the given source or from world knowledge, a phenomenon known as hallucination.In search engines, healthcare, legal and enterprise applications, the need for factually reliable LLM is now placed in the first place of the agenda of both the researchers and practitioners.This paper reviews the causes of hallucination, categorizes hallucination detection into reference-based and black-box families and examines different categories of approaches for mitigating hallucination from the training-time, retrieval-augmented, decoding-time and post-hoc verification.In addition to this survey, we conduct a comparative study of six mitigation setups and five detection techniques for short-form question answering and long-form generation.The rate of hallucination decreases by about 66.7% from direct prompting for long-form generation by retrieval-augmented generation and post-hoc verification, and by smaller and complementary amounts by contrastive decoding and chain-of-verification.Retrieval-grounded factual-precision scoring outperforms consistency-based black-box detection approaches, which rely on no knowledge of the model's inner workings, when it comes to sentence-level detection accuracy among the detection methods.We find that none of the single-behaviour systems are found to be capable of eliminating hallucination and that the most reliable systems are those that use a training-time or decoding-time intervention followed by an external, retrievalgrounded verification step.

candidates.title: GRaSP: Latency-Aware Optimization for Geo-Distributed Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is increasingly served across geo-distributed cloud and edge infrastructures, where wide-area latency, cross-region egress cost, and data-residency rules compete with retrieval quality. Conventional pipelines rank by semantic similarity alone and ignore where content lives, inflating tail latency and cost. We formalize the Geo-RAG Selection Problem (GRaSP), a drop-in re-scoring layer that decays relevance by latency and adds an optional cost penalty under a cardinality budget and per-region caps, with no retraining. We first settle its complexity: the base formulation is a linear objective over a partition matroid, solved optimally by an O(N log N) greedy algorithm, rather than NP-hard as a knapsack framing suggests, with hardness entering only under an additive egress budget. On a five-node CloudLab testbed emulating a four-region WAN over the Natural Questions corpus (2.68M passages), GRaSP's benefit is placement-dependent: under uniform placement it cuts fetch latency at negligible quality cost; under topical (residency-like) placement it traces a recall-latency Pareto frontier that dominates relevance-only, nearest-k, and a latency-budgeted baseline. At a moderate latency setting, GRaSP lowers P90 fetch latency by 41% while retaining 78% of relevance-only's recall, with sub-millisecond selection overhead, stable to 200 queries/s. Findings generalize across four public BEIR benchmarks. In end-to-end question answering, GRaSP reduces context-fetch latency by 43% while remaining within 0.062 absolute EM of relevance-only retrieval.

candidates.title: Evaluating Large Language Models in conceptual modeling: An experimental design
candidates.abstract: Conceptual modeling is instrumental in data engineering and knowledge representation. With the increasing adoption of Large Language Models in data-centric tasks, their capacity to generate conceptual models, such as Entity-Relationship Diagrams, continues to require attention. This paper evaluates the performance of Large Language Models in defining Entity-Relationship Diagrams from datasets. To this end, we designed a reproducible experimental framework in which two models of different natures (Mistral Small and Gemini 2.5 Flash) and a deterministic profiling baseline without any language model are evaluated on two datasets, under a full combined scenarios that crosses three types of expert knowledge (a domain description, an attribute-level data dictionary, and business rules) with three levels of informativeness of the attributes’ names, at three sampling temperatures with replicated executions. In summary, 864 generated models, plus six deterministic baseline evaluations, for a total of 870 evaluated models, all scored automatically against reference models curated by domain experts, across entities, relationships, keys, and attributes. The results show that no knowledge type is universally the most effective, that more knowledge is not necessarily better, that the benefit of expert knowledge varies between the two evaluated models and across datasets, and that the informativeness of the attributes’ names, rather than their mere presence, conditions the results; temperature affects the reproducibility of the outputs more than their quality. These findings help to delimit the roles of the data, the language model, and the domain expert in conceptual modeling. The complete experiment is available as a public replication package.

candidates.title: DiffuPlan: Editable Planning State for Diffusion Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) are emerging as an alternative to autoregressive (AR) language models, yet dLLM agents largely inherit an interaction protocol designed for AR generation: once intermediate state is written, later observations can only be incorporated by appending more text. This is a poor match to a defining capability of dLLMs -- reconstructing earlier text conditioned on context that appears both before and after it. We ask whether this capability can support a different agent-state paradigm in which intermediate planning state is directly revisable as evidence arrives. We introduce DiffuPlan, a diffusion search agent that maintains a single editable planning state and reconstructs only the affected steps when later evidence resolves an entity or changes the search route. To support variable-length revisions, we introduce Expansion-Partition Marginalization (EPM), which marginalizes over equivalent expansion paths. We further adapt diffusion trajectory RL to multi-turn search. Across four multi-hop QA benchmarks, DiffuPlan achieves 50.24 average F1, outperforming strong AR search agents. More importantly, under identical data and training, editable planning state improves the diffusion agent by 2.44 F1 versus only 0.47 for its AR source model. These results show that dLLMs need not imitate append-only AR agents: revising committed state is a distinct agentic advantage.

candidates.title: Comparing BM25, Multilingual-E5, and Reciprocal Rank Fusion for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) incorporates externally retrieved information as contextual knowledge to improve the quality of responses generated by language models. However, a RAG system's effectiveness depends heavily on the retrieval method's ability to identify and rank relevant documents. This study compares BM25, Multilingual-E5, and a hybrid approach based on Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) using a product and service catalog corpus consisting of 145 documents and 40 benchmark queries. The evaluation was conducted in two stages: retrieval performance was assessed using Hit@1, Hit@3, Hit@5, and MRR@5, while RAG answer quality was evaluated using Faithfulness, Answer Relevancy, and Answer Accuracy. The results show that BM25 achieved the highest Hit@1 score (0.775) and MRR@5 (0.8279), whereas Multilingual-E5 achieved the highest Hit@5 score (0.950). For answer quality, Multilingual-E5 obtained the highest Faithfulness score (0.9667), while the hybrid RRF approach achieved the highest Answer Relevancy score (0.8451); both achieved an Answer Accuracy score (0.7938). Statistical tests revealed no significant differences among the retrieval methods. Answer Relevancy and Answer Accuracy were descriptively lower when the target document was absent from the Top-5 context, whereas the target's exact position within ranks 1-5 showed no significant correlation with answer quality. A context-size robustness analysis further showed descriptive improvements in Answer Relevancy and Answer Accuracy from Top-1 to Top-3 and Top-5, although none of the nine context-size effects remained statistically significant after Holm correction. Under a criterion emphasizing Top-5 target coverage and downstream answer quality, Multilingual-E5 showed a favorable operational profile under the evaluated configuration.

candidates.title: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Zero-Shot Human–Object Interaction
candidates.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong zero-shot reasoning across diverse domains, but their potential for Human-Object Interaction (HOI) remains unexplored. Unlike traditional HOI approaches that rely on extensive labeled datasets and fixed interaction taxonomies, MLLMs offer flexible reasoning, making them well-suited for dynamic, real-world scenarios. In this work, we present the first systematic study of MLLMs for HOI recognition and detection within a pipeline that combines an external object detector for entity localization with zero-shot multimodal reasoning for interaction understanding. We introduce a benchmark framework for principled zero-shot evaluation, consisting of (i) a unified taxonomy of zero-shot prompting strategies, and (ii) a methodology that transforms token-level logits into interaction scores, enabling fair comparison with specialized HOI models under standard metrics. To support prompt-based evaluation, we additionally construct new question–answer annotations for standard HOI datasets, transforming them into a format suitable for MLLMs. Building on this, we propose two visual prompting strategies, namely Objects as Context and Black Other Objects, that guide MLLMs to target objects while preserving scene context. Experiments on HICO, HICO-DET, and V-COCO demonstrate state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, achieving 53.50 mAP on HICO and 23.69 mAP on HICO-DET. Overall, our work provides a principled benchmarking framework for MLLMs in HOI, opening the door to new models and datasets and enabling flexible open-world interaction understanding. Code and adapted datasets are publicly available. 1

candidates.title: VisConf: Quality-Aware Consensus for Best-of-N in Vision-Language Model Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Best-of-N methods improve text-only LLM reasoning by sampling multiple trajectories before selecting an answer. For Vision-Language Models (VLMs), answer frequency and model confidence alone can be insufficient, as sampled generations also vary in their engagement with the visual input. We find that distributional confidence and visual attention are complementary indicators of rollout quality. Each is limited on its own, while trajectories that show strong signals in both are more likely to be correct. Motivated by this, we introduce VisConf, a rollout-quality score that multiplicatively combines visual engagement with candidate-calibrated Self-Certainty, penalizing rollouts that are weak in either signal. We incorporate Rank-Weighted Consensus (RWC), a tuning-free aggregation rule that converts within-question VisConf ranks into answer-level vote weights. Across three VLMs on MathVista, MMMU-Pro, and MMStar, VisConf with RWC consistently outperforms strong BoN baselines. Our analysis shows particularly large gains when correct trajectories are present but underrepresented in the candidate pool.

candidates.title: Koi: Evidence-Guided, Self-Calibrating Planning for Multi-Cloud, Heterogeneous LLM Inference Fleets
candidates.abstract: Deploying a large language model (LLM) requires choosing the right accelerator, parallelization strategy, engine configuration, and replica count amongst ~140 other variables across clouds, regions, and markets. These decisions are intertwined, and the best cluster-wide plan continually changes as jobs contend for shared capacity on shifting workloads. We present Koi, a self-calibrating cluster planner for heterogeneous, multi-cloud fleets. Koi uses a Recursive Language Model (RLM) hierarchy to propose hypotheses and reason over deployment while deterministic components predict serving behavior, score candidates, and control placement. It represents inference behavior as a fixed causal graph linking decisions (e.g., accelerator, parallelism), runtime mediators (e.g., KV-cache pressure, communication overhead), and outcomes (e.g., latency, throughput). Each deployment strengthens or weakens scoped causal relationships, building a comprehensive playbook for inference that the planner employs to guide future decisions. Job-wise configurations are composed into cluster-wide plans and evaluated against serving objectives, resource constraints, SLO risks, and cost. Across benchmarks, Koi achieves 1.18x greater goodput than the strongest baseline while reducing $/token by 20% in a real heterogeneous cluster. Ablations isolate the contribution of Koi's architecture: a pure language model attains a composite score of 35.3, the same model equipped with Koi's deterministic tools reaches 51.6, and the full Koi planner reaches 70.8.

candidates.title: The Impact of Retrieval Augmented Generation on the Reliability of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable fluency but remain fundamentally unreliable for knowledge-intensive tasks due to hallucination, temporal staleness, and lack of verifiability.Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a dominant architectural paradigm that grounds generation in external evidence.This paper provides a comprehensive investigation into how RAG reshapes LLM reliability across factual accuracy, citation fidelity, temporal freshness, and robustness to noise.We benchmark five RAG variants against closed-book baselines using secondary datasets including Natural Questions, TriviaQA, HotpotQA, and RGB.Results show an average 23.7% reduction in hallucination rate and 31.2%improvement in citation grounding when using advanced retrieval with self-reflection.However, we identify critical failure modes: retriever-generator misalignment, context distraction, and over-reliance on irrelevant passages.We propose a reliability framework and demonstrate that corrective and modular RAG designs significantly mitigate these risks.Our findings establish RAG as necessary but not sufficient for trustworthy deployment.

candidates.title: Governable agentic intelligence: a lifecycle framework linking capability, assurance, and oversight in large language model agents
candidates.abstract: Abstract Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) embeds large language models (LLMs) in action loops in which they plan, retrieve evidence, invoke tools, maintain memory, coordinate with other agents, and change external state. Reviews of this field have proliferated, yet they remain fragmented: architecture surveys catalogue components, evaluation surveys catalogue benchmarks, and safety surveys catalogue risks, while deployed agents couple all three. Scholars have yet to sufficiently examine how capability, evaluation, and governance interact within the lifecycle of a single agentic system. We address this gap through a critical review that codes 19 reviews and surveys published in Artificial Intelligence Review between 2024 and 2026 and situates them within foundational primary studies and cross-venue surveys. We argue that agency is a configurable property of a socio-technical control loop, not an attribute of a model. From the corpus, we develop the Agentic Intelligence Lifecycle (AIL), a six-layer framework spanning foundation, cognition, grounding, orchestration, evaluation, and governance. Our central finding is that every mechanism that expands capability also incurs an assurance debt : a gap between the risks the mechanism introduces and the controls that keep those risks observable and bounded. We theorize this relationship in five propositions, propose a five-question assurance model that shifts evaluation from outputs to trajectories and deployment conditions, and derive a ten-point research agenda for agentic systems that are observable, attributable, interruptible, and governable.

candidates.title: Characterising and Analysing Retrieval-Augmented Generation Techniques
candidates.abstract: The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) across many application domains has increased the need for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to reduce hallucinations and improve LLM performance. Thus far, several RAG techniques with impressive features and capabilities have been proposed in the literature, making it a herculean task to select the most appropriate RAG techniques for specific problem scenarios. Thus, we propose a conceptual framework comprising main dimensions and sub-dimensions for characterising (defining "what it is") and analysing (defining "how well it does") existing RAG techniques. The conceptual framework was developed through a qualitative analysis of the attributes of RAG techniques reported in the literature. It can serve as a pre-empirical filtering mechanism for researchers and practitioners in selecting the highest-fit RAG candidates that meet specific user and task requirements before empirical benchmarking of RAG techniques, which can be computationally and financially expensive.

candidates.title: On the Position Bias of Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Study
candidates.abstract: Recent studies have shown that position bias remains a critical vulnerability in large language models (LLMs), undermining both the integrity of multiple-choice evaluations and the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation. However, existing understanding of this phenomenon is largely derived from studies with limited model coverage and English-centric benchmarks, leaving the behavior of frontier models and diverse languages underexplored. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation of position bias across model scales ranging from billion-level to trillion-level parameters, covering both multiple-choice and multi-document tasks in five languages. Our experiments reveal that while position bias remains noticeable in small-scale models and Non-English languages, increasing model scale and employing standard Chain-of-Thought prompting significantly mitigate this issue. Moreover, we demonstrate that emerging \emph{thinking models} with extended reasoning capabilities are nearly immune to position bias, suggesting a costly but general approach toward resolving this vulnerability.

candidates.title: Who Pays for Efficient Inference? Confidence-Based Small-to-Large LLM Routing Across Tasks and Languages
candidates.abstract: Small-to-large language model routing can reduce inference cost by escalating difficult inputs while retaining easier ones on a smaller model. Its success, however, depends on identifying examples that benefit from escalation, and the reliability of confidence across multilingual tasks remains unclear. We present a systematic evaluation of confidence-based routing across three model families, four languages, and three task types, covering 72 model, dataset, language, and scale configurations and 42,288 predictions. We compare global confidence routing with random routing, equal-quota confidence routing, and an oracle upper bound. Confidence identifies beneficial escalations on the Belebele reading comprehension and SIB-200 topic classification datasets, with mean correction-detection AUCs of 0.612 and 0.705. At 50% escalation, it improves over random routing by 1.40--4.67 percentage points on Belebele and 2.54--5.63 points on SIB-200. In contrast, the mean AUC on the MMLU-ProX-Lite knowledge and reasoning dataset is only 0.510, and routing provides no consistent improvement over random selection because small models often remain highly confident while incorrect. Global confidence routing also creates language escalation gaps up to 30.33 percentage points, whereas equal-quota routing removes this disparity with little aggregate accuracy cost. These results show that confidence routing is task-dependent and can allocate computation unevenly across languages. Code is available at https://github.com/sabbir5622r/multilingual-llm-routing

candidates.title: Under the Skin: Backdoor Infection in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance in generating text conditioned on inputs from different modalities. In this work, we introduce backdoor infection, a cross-modal attack framework targeting MLLMs. Starting from a model already injected with a backdoor in one modality, our attack constructs a corresponding trigger in another modality, called the infected modality. Exploiting the model's shared latent space, the trigger in the infected modality reliably activates the malicious behavior, without modifying or poisoning the infected modality during training. We further develop a lightweight, constraint-aware optimization method for efficient and practical trigger generation. Extensive experiments across several state-of-the-art MLLMs, including LLaVA, InternVL, Qwen-VL, and Gemma, demonstrate that our approach identifies cross-modal triggers that are more efficient, effective, and less detectable than direct optimization baselines, highlighting a critical new threat vector in multimodal systems.

candidates.title: Towards efficient large language models for scientific data: a review
candidates.abstract: Abstract The adaptation of large language models (LLMs) to scientific domains requires efficient strategies to mitigate high computational costs while preserving performance. We present a systematic survey of efficiency techniques for adapting LLMs to scientific applications. Our review analyzes 120 studies across seven scientific fields, including biomedicine, clinical medicine, biology, mathematics, chemistry, geo-environmental science, and cross-domain scientific research. Across the surveyed literature, we summarize 34 representative models and 30 scientific datasets for efficient scientific LLM research. Examining parameter-efficient fine-tuning, knowledge distillation, architectural optimization, and data-centric approaches, we introduce a dual-axis taxonomy that organizes efficiency techniques by both methodological strategy and scientific domain. We further provide practical guidance for selecting efficiency strategies under resource constraints and highlight open challenges including multimodal integration, catastrophic forgetting, and automated method selection. By synthesizing cross-domain evidence and outlining directions for sustainable model development, this survey supports the adoption of efficient scientific LLMs in resource-constrained research environments and promotes more accessible and responsible deployment across scientific disciplines.

candidates.title: Revisiting the Federalist Papers in the Era of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: For a long time, the authorship of the Federalist Papers had been a subject of inquiry and debate, not only by linguists and historians but also by statisticians. In what was arguably the first Bayesian case study, Mosteller and Wallace (1963) provided the first statistical evidence for attributing all disputed papers to Madison. Our paper revisits this historical dataset through the lens of modern language models alongside classical statistical language models. We review some of the more widely used neural embedding-based models, which are often trained on massive, general-purpose corpora, and examine them from a statistical point of view in the context of text classification. We investigate whether, without any task-specific fine-tuning, these high-dimensional contextual embeddings can be useful for authorship attribution and to identify writing-style features. We contrast these with classical, likelihood-based models that produce low-dimensional, interpretable representations grounded in explicit probabilistic structure. Contrary to our expectations, we find that extremely high-dimensional contextual embeddings do not necessarily outperform interpretable, lower-dimensional topic-based embeddings for attribution. Our experiments show that default neural embeddings (even after manual fine-tuning) may not consistently improve authorship attribution accuracy. Instead, Bayesian analysis using latent topic embeddings derived from “function words” yields superior out-of-sample classification performance, underscoring that interpretable statistical language models, with their theoretical grounding, can offer significant advantages in authorship attribution. The code used in this analysis is available at github.com/sowonjeong/slm-2-llm <github.com/sowonjeong/slm-2-llm>

candidates.title: Coopshift: Post-Training Amplifies The Memory Curse In LLM Cooperation
candidates.abstract: How does post-training change cooperation during repeated interaction? Within each of seven released model lineages, we compare pretrained (Base), supervised fine-tuned (SFT), and subsequent preference- or reward-optimized (Aligned) checkpoints across seven social dilemmas. Copies of each checkpoint play one another for 200 rounds, with visible history limited to the last two or forty rounds. The memory curse refers to lower cooperation when agents can see more past rounds. Our central finding is that post-training amplifies this decline. Averaged across the six binary-action games, expanding visible history reduces cooperation at every SFT and Aligned checkpoint. At each post-trained stage, these declines exceed Base's in six of seven lineages. Most of this average amplification is already present at SFT. With long history, both post-trained stages also cooperate less than Base on average in each binary-action game. In the symmetric binary games, their fitted cooperation rates fall more steeply on average than Base's as per-round cooperation costs rise, benefits fall, or noncooperation becomes more rewarding. The difference in cooperation rates between Aligned and SFT also changes from one-shot decisions to repeated play. When given the same past records, their choices depend on whether the instructions describe a final round or possible future interaction. Post-training evaluation should therefore go beyond isolated choices to assess whether cooperation is sustained in repeated interaction and how it depends on payoffs and visible history.

candidates.title: Competence-Based Evaluation of Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have brought impressive performance across diverse tasks; however, shortcomings remain in logical reasoning, including inconsistencies under linguistic variation. To improve the reasoning capacity of LLMs, we must be able to accurately measure their reasoning capacity. Current benchmarks primarily report single accuracy numbers on selected reasoning tasks. Such a performance-based evaluation methodology says little about a model's generalization capacity in reasoning. To address this limitation, we argue for a different evaluation paradigm, called competence-based evaluation (CBE), which tests whether models reliably apply the same competence across a family of problems. A parameterized generator scales complexity while keeping the required competence fixed, and matched answer-preserving presentations test correctness beyond one formulation. We instantiate CBE on elementary ordering tasks, scaling input size while varying presentations of the same ordering rule. Across six GPT and Qwen models, performance is reasonably good over bounded complexity ranges, but even strong models fail the competence condition across the tested family. Chain-of-thought and GRPO extend strong performance without resolving all tested failures; supervised LoRA shows little held-out transfer. CBE provides diagnostic profiles and an evaluation protocol that can grow with future models.

candidates.title: Prism Attention: Proposal-Refined Index Sharing Mechanism for Efficient LLMs Inference
candidates.abstract: Long-context decoding in large language models (LLMs) is increasingly bottlenecked by the memory and computation required to attend over an ever-growing Key-Value (KV) cache at each autoregressive step. Although token-level sparse attention reduces this burden by restricting computation to a small subset of relevant past tokens, its practical gains are often offset by repeatedly recomputing layer-wise sparse indices as the context grows. A common remedy is to share sparse indices across layers by computing them only at designated anchor layers, but such static reuse ignores the layer-wise evolution of attention patterns, causing the reused indices to progressively deviate from the layer-specific optima and incur substantial attention loss. By revisiting cross-layer sparsity from the perspective of attention dynamics, we find that inter-layer salient token shift is highly localized: although the exact top-$κ$ indices differ across layers, the core high-attention tokens remain stable, with changes concentrated near the expanded boundary of previously selected regions. Motivated by this, we propose Prism Attention, a proposal-refined sparse attention framework. It replaces rigid cross-layer index reuse with a coarse-to-fine strategy, preserving layer-wise adaptability while retaining the efficiency benefits of cross-layer sharing. Extensive experiments show that Prism Attention achieves state-of-the-art performance among mainstream sparse attention methods on both reasoning and long-context benchmarks, while attaining a $3.4\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup over FlashAttention at 128K context length.

candidates.title: FLARE: Physics-Grounded Evaluation of Language-Model Agents for Feeder Restoration with Degraded Observations
candidates.abstract: Restoring service after distribution-grid faults requires decisions from incomplete and conflicting information while respecting electrical constraints. Addressing this need, we introduce FLARE (Feeder-Level Agent Restoration Evaluation), a physics-grounded benchmark for post-isolation feeder restoration. FLARE con- tains 800 AC-feasible cases across five observation settings and allows agents to gather evidence, evaluate switches, and perform restoration actions under fixed operational limits. We evaluate five instruction-tuned models over 78,750 episodes, including topology, distributed-generation, and loading shifts. Mean normalized regret ranges from 0.082 to 0.148. Although every model has zero median regret, P95 regret ranges from 0.814 to 1.000, revealing an important failure tail. Shadow replay shows that 96.4% of 15,706 guard-rejected actions would have caused a physical violation. FLARE enables reproducible evaluation of language-model based restoration support while emphasizing the need for external safety checks.

candidates.title: Uncertainty-Aware Budget Allocation for Efficient LLM Tree Search
candidates.abstract: Tree search enhances multi-step reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet prevailing methods expand every step with a fixed budget, irrespective of the marginal utility of expansion. We first show, across existing search algorithms, that continuations sampled from a shared intermediate state are largely duplicates and collapse to a few distinct answers. Critically, we find that the semantic dispersion of sibling actions predicts the redundancy of their downstream continuations, permitting a subtree's budget to be fixed before expansion. An information-theoretic analysis motivates this: treating the per-step budget as the Monte Carlo sample size for estimating a step's residual answer entropy, we derive a sufficient budget that shrinks with sibling dispersion. We accordingly propose $\textbf{Uncertainty-Aware Allocation}$ (UAA), a training-free framework that decouples value from uncertainty: values determine which candidates are promising, while uncertainty, estimated from sibling dispersion at no additional model cost, determines how many merit expansion, via uncertainty-aware pruning and uncertainty-aware budgeting. Across mathematical reasoning, logical reasoning, and planning benchmarks, UAA reduces token usage by up to $90\%$ and latency by up to $9\times$ at comparable accuracy, generalizing across four tree search algorithms and both open- and closed-source LLMs.

candidates.title: Language Models Learn to Improve Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate AI research, including language-model (LM) development, offering a potential path toward recursive self-improvement. However, turning experimental feedback into a learned ability to propose effective improvements across models faces two challenges. First, training such an ability with real feedback is expensive: reinforcement learning (RL) requires evaluating tens of thousands of proposals, each potentially requiring a full model-training run. Even at ten GPU-hours per run, reward collection alone would consume hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours, motivating a cheaper surrogate. Second, surrogate feedback can become unreliable as policy optimization favors overestimated proposals when the proposal distribution shifts. To address these challenges, we propose LM2LM, which trains LLMs with RL to generate effective LM improvement proposals. To provide scalable feedback, we use a research world model (RWM), a frozen LLM that predicts proposal gains from real experimental records provided in context, as the reward model for RL. To maintain feedback reliability, we periodically execute current-policy proposals ranked highly by the RWM and add their measured outcomes to its context. Across eight autoregressive and diffusion LM development environments, real-execution evaluations on held-out tasks show that LM2LM enables Qwen3.8-27B to outperform GPT-6-sol, even when GPT-6-sol is given 300 real experimental records in context, while requiring 33% lower data-generation cost. LM2LM also generalizes to a model family unseen during training.

candidates.title: KiranaBench: Can a Language Model Run a Neighbourhood Shop?
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly evaluated on long-horizon tasks, including autonomously running a business. Existing benchmarks for this setting are almost exclusively English-language, Western in retail context, and single-agent, with the agent observing the business directly. We study how these results transfer to a multi-agent Indic setting. We introduce KiranaBench, a simulated Indian general store in which four roles (manager, cashier, helper, and bookkeeper) are each played by a separate LLM agent. Interactions with customers and suppliers occur in English, Hindi, or Hinglish, and product demand is calibrated to India's national Household Consumption Expenditure Survey. Evaluating four open-weight LLMs, we find that all fall far short of a fixed-rule shopkeeper baseline: the best model earns only one-eighth of the baseline's profit, and two models finish below an unmanaged shop. Performance is also consistently lower for Hindi and Hinglish than for English supplier communication. KiranaBench offers evidence that current LLM agents are not yet reliable for autonomously operating small businesses in India, and provides a testbed for developing agents suited to settings that are long-horizon, collaborative, and multilingual.

candidates.title: Efficient and Effective Test Generation and Type Inference for Python Applications
candidates.abstract: Python has become one of the most widely used programming languages, valued for its flexibility and ease of use. However, its dynamic nature provides only limited static guarantees, making programs more difficult to write reliably: errors are more likely to remain undetected until runtime. Tests and type checking can mitigate these issues by detecting bugs—including runtime errors—before release, but creating tests and the type annotations required for checking demands substantial developer effort, discouraging their widespread use. Approaches to automating test generation and type inference are hindered not only by Python’s dynamic features but also by the substantial performance limitations of CPython, the standard Python interpreter, which make dynamic analysis costly in practice. In this dissertation, I explore how low-overhead dynamic analysis can be used to improve the reliability of Python software. First, I introduce SlipCover, a code coverage measurement tool that significantly reduces runtime overhead through efficient bytecode instrumentation and dynamic de-instrumentation. SlipCover enables practical use of coverage tracking in iterative workflows by achieving near-zero overhead, supporting a range of software engineering applications. Building on SlipCover, I next present CoverUp, a regression test generation tool that uses coverage feedback to efficiently guide a large language model in generating unit tests that significantly outperform previous methods in coverage. Finally, I propose RightTyper, an efficient and effective type annotation system. RightTyper combines types observed through low-overhead, statistically guided runtime sampling with static analysis and name resolution to produce type annotations comparable in quality to current LLM-based approaches and substantially better than those of all other evaluated tools—while remaining grounded in observed program behavior rather than probabilistic inference. Collectively, these contributions advance the state of the art by showing how low-overhead dynamic analysis helps overcome significant challenges in writing and maintaining reliable Python code.

candidates.title: Data Optimization for LLMs: A Survey
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have attracted great attention in both academic and industrial communities in recent years. Numerous survey studies have covered various aspects of LLMs, such as learning strategies, applications, alignment, explainability, and evaluation. However, little headway has been made in reviewing data-related aspects for LLMs, despite data being recognized as a key factor contributing to the emergence of the LLMs era. A wide range of data optimization algorithms and techniques are employed in LLMs' training and application processes. These techniques often originate from diverse deep learning domains, with their theoretical inspirations and heuristic motivations appearing unrelated to each other. This study aims to develop a comprehensive framework for LLMs' data optimization techniques to enhance data utilization efficiency. We first discuss data challenges in LLMs' training and inference. Second, we summarize data perception dimensions for evaluating LLMs' data properties. Third, existing optimization techniques are reviewed and categorized into four groups: data selection, augmentation, reweighting, and others. Fourth, we analyze interconnections between these categories. Finally, we identify key challenges and future directions for LLMs' data optimization compared with conventional deep learning approaches.

candidates.title: TEM: Temporal State Tracking Memory for Large Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: An agent's memory must remain useful as information changes across conversations. A new fact may replace an earlier value without making that value irrelevant to a later question. We present Temporal State Tracking Memory (TEM), a training-free framework for tracking these changes. TEM stores facts as versioned records linked to their sources. It retrieves relevant versions, places them in source order and labels historical records before passing the evidence to the answer model. Event memory and original dialogue turns provide details missing from structured facts. We evaluated TEM on 420 questions drawn from 600 sessions involving 60 personas. Across four open-weight models, key-entity hit rates reached 75.71-97.62% overall and 96.67-100.00% on the historical-residence subset. Adding historical labels to otherwise identical, source-ordered facts increased overall hit rates by 17.14-55.95 percentage points. The evidence was compact: 94-118 tokens per answer, or 48.75-56.73% less than session-aware retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). A further evaluation on 1,540 LoCoMo questions tested hybrid memory under a fixed evidence budget. TEM exceeded session-aware RAG with both backbones; conservative score differences were 7.92 and 10.58 percentage points. The results support preserving fact versions and exposing their temporal status to the generator when answering questions about repeatedly updated information.

candidates.title: Managing Vector Data for Retrieval Augmented Generation@Dagstuhl Seminar Summary
candidates.abstract: This report summarizes discussions that took place in the context of a Dagstuhl seminar1 to explore the emerging paradigm of AI-native databases designed to support agentic workflows and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) by integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with robust database abstractions. The central synthesis of the Dagstuhl discussions is the necessary evolution of databases from passive vector stores into active data-native agentic harnesses that orchestrate AI reasoning and task-centric execution. A recurring lesson across keynotes and working groups is that achieving mission-critical reliability requires integrating AI primitives, such as embeddings, model inference, and semantic operators, as first-class citizens while maintaining traditional database guarantees like transactional consistency, explainability, and cost-aware optimization. This transition necessitates a structured approach to agent memory (spanning episodic, semantic, and procedural scales) and a shift toward adaptive, iterative execution models that go beyond static query planning to accommodate the stochastic nature of foundation models. There is a community consensus that reliability, responsibility, and security (specifically addressing compositional leakage) must be treated as end-to-end concerns supported by holistic benchmarks that evaluate the entire quality chain from retrieval to autonomous action.

candidates.title: A Systematic Review of Hallucination Mitigation in Large Language Models Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become widely used for question answering, education, research, summarization and information support. Despite their usefulness, LLMs may generate false, unsupported or inconsistent information, commonly described as hallucination. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses this reliability problem by retrieving relevant information from external knowledge sources and supplying it to the language model as contextual evidence before generating a response. This paper studies the role of RAG in reducing factual hallucinations through a review of existing research and a 50 question pilot comparison of responses generated with and without retrieval support. The submitted report records 49 of 50 responses as correct without RAG and all 50 as correct with RAG; it separately presents a clearly labelled illustrative distribution of 46/3/1 versus 48/2/0 for demonstrating response categories. The distinction is retained to avoid presenting illustrative values as observed experimental results. The study also examines limitations including poor retrieval, unreliable sources, incomplete context and incorrect interpretation of retrieved evidence. The paper concludes that RAG is a practical hallucination-reduction approach, but it should be combined with high-quality retrieval, evidence verification and human oversight for critical applications.

candidates.title: Private Retrieval Augmented Generation via Random Projection
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) by querying external structured knowledge. However, it can also introduce privacy risks by leaking sensitive information from the retrieval datastore. We propose a simple method to preserve datastore privacy in RAG systems via random projection. By applying the same projection to both datastore embeddings and query embeddings, our method provably preserves semantic similarity between queries and retrieved items while substantially mitigating data extraction attacks. Across multiple RAG architectures and datasets, we show that this lightweight approach achieves superior retrieval and generation performance compared to prior methods which leverage formal differential privacy (DP) guarantees, while exhibiting comparable empirical privacy under strong attack models. Our results for the first time suggest that random projection can serve as a competitive and practical baseline for privacy-preserving RAG systems.

candidates.title: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): An Adaptive Framework for Evidence-Grounded Question Answering
candidates.abstract: This paper presents a proposed Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework for adaptive, evidence-grounded question answering using large language models (LLMs). Unlike conventional single-pass RAG systems, the proposed framework incorporates query planning, retrieval, tool selection, evidence evaluation, answer generation, and self-reflection. The framework uses a bounded feedback loop to improve evidence retrieval when the initial results are insufficient or conflicting. It aims to produce answers supported by relevant source citations while communicating uncertainty when reliable evidence is unavailable. The paper discusses the system architecture, workflow, algorithmic control logic, evaluation methodology, security, privacy, and governance considerations. It also proposes evaluation metrics for answer quality, retrieval effectiveness, factual grounding, latency, computational cost, and component-level ablation studies. Potential applications include research assistance, document question answering, enterprise knowledge management, customer support, and data analysis. This work presents a conceptual framework and proposed evaluation plan. Implementation, benchmark experiments, and measured performance improvements are not reported. Keywords: Agentic RAG, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Large Language Models, AI Agents, Evidence-Grounded Question Answering, Adaptive Retrieval, Self-Reflection.

candidates.title: Generative Models, Foundation Models and Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Most of the artificial intelligence described in this book answers a narrow question about an image. Three newer kinds of model do something broader. Generative models produce new images or text. Foundation models are trained once on very large and varied data and then adapted to many tasks with few labelled examples. Large language models, the best known of the foundation models, read and write text with a fluency that has surprised their makers. This chapter explains in plain terms how each of them works, what they are used for in medical imaging and what can go wrong. It covers the synthesis and translation of images, synthetic data, self-supervised pretraining, promptable segmentation, and the use of language models for reports, patient information and data extraction. Simulations computed for the chapter illustrate diffusion, synthetic data for a rare class, the removal of a lesion by a generative model, a miniature language model and the saving in labels from pretraining. The final sections deal with invented content, privacy, bias and the human checking that these tools require.

candidates.title: From Long Context to Selective Memory:A Survey of Memory-Centric Compression for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Long-context capability has become essential for large language models (LLMs) to handle complex tasks, yet continuously expanding the context window does not remove the computational, storage, and information-selection pressures incurred at inference time. Existing work on prompt compression, KV-cache management, efficient serving, retrieval augmentation, and agent memory is usually discussed in isolation, leaving the flow of information between storage and computation insufficiently understood. This survey reframes long-context compression as a memory-management problem for allocating inference-time resources. We distinguish compute-active memory, which directly participates in model computation, from compute-inactive memory, which lies outside the computation path but can be stored, retrieved, updated, or forgotten, and we characterize offloaded KV caches, persistent prefix caches, and precomputed KV states as intermediate states on the activation path. On this basis, we formulate writing, offloading, recall, retrieval-and-injection, materialization, eviction, consolidation, and forgetting as state transitions within an information lifecycle, and introduce a budgeted cost model that places these operations in a single cost account. The resulting framework unifies short-term context compression, long-term memory management, and the transitions between them, and shows that the central challenge is not merely reducing information volume but deciding which information should participate in costly inference, when, and in what form. We further summarize evaluation dimensions, benchmark gaps, and open challenges, and argue that future research should move from static, pointwise compression toward dynamic, governable, lifecycle-aware memory management.

candidates.title: ReFlow: Replay-Driven Decoupling for Efficient RL Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has been a critical paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) reasoning and agentic capabilities, but its efficiency remains a major bottleneck. Existing RL systems commonly rely on asynchronous execution to overlap rollout generation with policy optimization for enhanced efficiency. However, this approach faces inherent limitations: mild policy staleness offers only limited training efficiency gains, whereas aggressive asynchrony can degrade model quality and yields diminishing efficiency gains. The dynamic nature of LLM RL and multi-turn agentic workloads further challenges RL system design, as resource demands shift over time, making static resource allocation and generation strategy inefficient. This paper presents ReFlow, a system-algorithm co-designed RL framework for efficient LLM post-training. Its key insight is that, unlike existing RL frameworks which consume each trajectory only once, experience replay of recent trajectories enables effective sample reuse, thereby amortizing the high cost of rollout generation without incurring excessive policy staleness. To fully exploit this opportunity, ReFlow adopts a decoupled and adaptive architecture with three key designs: a dual replay data cycle supports efficient experience reuse while balancing training throughput and optimization stability; an elastic resource pool enables dynamic resource placement to accommodate evolving RL workloads; an adaptive scheduler coordinates generation strategies and resource allocation to improve resource utilization and boost generation throughput. Experiments across representative single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic RL tasks show that ReFlow improves training throughput by up to $2.06\times$ over state-of-the-art synchronous and asynchronous RL systems, while maintaining comparable or better model performance.

candidates.title: Data Strategies for Large Language Models: A Unified Perspective on the Training Lifecycle
candidates.abstract: Data strategy plays a central role in training large language models (LLMs). It governs the selection, weighting, and scheduling of training data, thereby determining the capabilities a model can acquire from a fixed data budget. We treat high-quality data as having high training-dependent utility, which depends on the target objective, the model, and its training state rather than on the text alone. Research in this area now spans pretraining and post-training, but related ideas use inconsistent terminology and evaluation protocols. This work reviews data strategies across the training lifecycle and formulates them as policies that allocate a training budget over candidate examples. We organise methods by their decision granularity, model dependence, and temporal adaptivity, then compare their computational requirements and empirical support. Fine-grained or state-dependent policies offer more control but incur additional scoring, search, or rollout costs. Evidence for transfer across model scales and comparable end-to-end cost remains limited. A continuously updated list of papers, along with their public implementations, is available at https://github.com/xuyj233/data_strategy_survey.

candidates.title: Fractional Power-of-Two Quantization for Efficient and Effective Multiplier-Free LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demand efficient inference, where the multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations in linear projections dominate compute and energy cost. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces this cost by mapping weights and activations to low-bit integers. Power-of-Two (PoT) weight quantization promises efficient multiplier-free LLM inference via shift-add logic, but suffers significant accuracy degradation at low bitwidths due to its coarse base-2 quantization grid. We introduce Fractional PoT (FPoT), a base-$\sqrt{2}$ (half-octave) fractional PoT grid that achieves practical 4-bit weight quantization while preserving a fully integer shift-add datapath. The method combines (i) the base-$\sqrt{2}$ weight grid with uniform integer activations, (ii) a calibration-time grid-alignment refinement absorbed into the static per-channel scale, and (iii) a lightweight 1-adder $\sqrt{2}$ approximation whose error is absorbed during weight calibration via approximate-grid quantization, yielding a processing element (PE) with significantly fewer gates than a 4-bit integer multiplier. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weight and activation quantization, FPoT improves zero-shot commonsense reasoning performance by 8.72% relative to the PoT baseline, while maintaining performance close to the uniform integer baseline, with only a negligible 0.4%p degradation. These results hold across various configurations spanning seven models and three bit-widths. Furthermore, FPoT can be integrated with state-of-the-art LLM PTQ methods, demonstrating framework-agnostic applicability.

candidates.title: Textbook-Enriched Training for Language Models: Boosting Answer Quality in Specialized Contexts
candidates.abstract: The use of textbooks as primary sources of information has increasingly given way to tools based on Large Language Models (LLMs), raising concerns about the reliability of generated answers. This study investigates how different adaptation strategies shape the behavior of small language models in educational Question Answering (QA) tasks in Portuguese. To support this analysis, we built a question-answer dataset derived from an NLP textbook and compared base models and the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline with models adapted through supervised fine-tuning and Continued Pretraining. The evaluation relies on questions from the LARI dataset, which has been validated by human specialists, and combines automatic and qualitative assessment procedures. The findings indicate that small models tuned with structured instructional knowledge achieve stronger semantic alignment and produce more pertinent answers in Portuguese educational QA scenarios.

candidates.title: When Reasoning Is Not Enough: Proactive Inquiry for Cross-Modal Safety in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can act unsafely when individually benign images and texts are interpreted jointly. Beyond implicit reasoning risk, where reasoning drifts toward harm, we identify intent-level risk, where cross-modal ambiguity silently commits the model to a hazardous premise that path-level optimization alone cannot correct. We propose SAFE-PRO, which uses a Risk-Conditioned Uncertainty (RCU) signal, combining predictive entropy with a learned cross-modal risk score, to decide when to ask safety-grounded clarifying questions and where to apply path optimization, under a reward that prioritizes safety and penalizes over-refusal. We also build SSUI-Dialog, a multimodal multi-turn dataset with dual-intent supervision, and theoretically analyze gradient variance and unsafe-completion risk under RCU. Across seven benchmarks and two base MLLMs, SAFE-PRO consistently improves safety over SRPO, roughly halves its over-refusal, and surpasses GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet in average single-turn safety.

candidates.title: The Expressive Power of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models process vast sequences of input tokens by alternating between classical multi-layer perceptron layers and self-attention mechanisms. While the approximation capabilities of perceptrons are relatively well understood, those of attention mechanisms remain less explored. In this talk, I will compare the proof techniques and approximation results associated with these two types of layers, emphasizing key open questions that connect large language models with approximation theory in infinite-dimensional spaces representing input token distributions.

candidates.title: The Density of Thought: Predicting and Steering Reasoning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: We investigate whether variation in information density across chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning steps predicts answer correctness and can serve as a controllable inference-time target. We prompt frozen pretrained models to solve problems via CoT and measure the density of each reasoning step with two independent metrics: LP variance (how unevenly information is distributed across steps, computed as the variance in mean per-token negative log-likelihood) and the Caveman compression ratio. We then test whether density correlates with, and can be steered to improve, answer correctness. Experiments across six model scales, two training paradigms, and 60 GSM8K problems yield four main findings. First, lower LP variance predicts correctness in supervised fine-tuned (SFT) models, but this relationship weakens with scale and reverses in reinforcement-learning (RL) distilled models. Training paradigm therefore appears more influential than model size in determining density behaviour. Second, synthetic experiments reveal an intrinsic complexity preference: models trained on uniformly distributed data learn complexity-favouring distributions 2.0 to 2.6 times more accurately than simplicity-favouring ones. Third, direct inference-time density steering reduces accuracy from 60.0% to 8.3%, indicating that natural density patterns are functionally important to reasoning. Fourth, pre-generation nudging combining hint injection with contrastive KV-cache steering improves accuracy by 13.3 percentage points, consistent across both metrics. Finally, we introduce Entropy-Gated Density Routing (EGDR), a self-supervised method using token-level Shannon entropy to gate proportional KVcache adjustments during generation, improving accuracy by 10.0 percentage points without any external guidance.

candidates.title: Name-Bias in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Names carry demographic indicators such as age, gender, and race, which makes them a subtle but strong target of bias in large language models (LLMs). In this work, we present an evaluation of name-based bias across 6 local large language models spanning multiple providers and parameter scales. Using a fill-in-the-blank task, we prompt these models to choose between pairs of first names drawn from U.S. Social Security Administration datasets and a race classification dataset by Rosenman et al.. Our experimental de- sign isolates age and gender effects through balanced name pairings and sentence templates that share a fixed syntactic structure. Across 300,000 local LLM responses, we find consistent and measurable name bias. Models prefer names that are less stereotypically male, older, popular, and white. Furthermore, we find that name-bias is highly sentence-dependent, but not more than associated stereotypes, and gender is the most significant bias, followed by age, name popularity, and race. Our results demonstrate that name-based bias remains pervasive even in local LLMs, highlighting the necessity for standardized evaluation methods and mitigation strategies.
